technical_sections.heading: 1. Taxonomy and Classification
technical_sections.body: Full hierarchy: Kingdom Animalia, Order Orthoptera, Suborder Ensifera, Superfamily Tettigonioidea, Family Tettigoniidae, Subfamily Hetrodinae, Tribe Acanthoplini, Genus Acanthoplus, species discoidalis (Walker, 1869) (Source: Orthoptera Species File, otus/844211). The species was originally described as Hetrodes discoidalis Walker, 1869, in the Catalogue of the Specimens of Dermaptera Saltatoria in the Collection of the British Museum (Source: OSF, otus/844211/overview). Several subjective synonyms were later folded in by Uvarov (1928): Hetrodes pallidus Walker, 1869; Acanthoplus desertorum Kirby, 1899; A. germanus Kirby, 1899; A. jallae Griffini, 1897; A. armativentris Pringuey, 1916; A. serratus; and A. bechuanus (the name still used in Power's 1958 behavioural work) (Source: OSF; Green 2002, DFID Report R7428). Type material is held at the Natural History Museum, London, and Iziko Museums, Cape Town, with historical collecting localities including "road from Kazungula to Bulawayo" and "Tuli" (Source: OSF, otus/844211). The genus Acanthoplus (Stl, 1873) comprises 16 species (Source: SANBI, Armoured bush cricket). Placement history: Zeuner's (1936) classification grouped Hetrodinae with Bradyporinae and Acridoxeninae under the "Bradyporoid" division of primitive katydids  the root of the older "Bradyporidae" name still occasionally seen for this group. Modern molecular phylogenetics instead places Hetrodinae as a monophyletic subfamily within Tettigoniidae (Source: Mugleston et al. 2018, Insect Systematics and Diversity 2(4):5). In that study's sampled taxon table, Hetrodinae is represented by 4 of its 5 tribes and 4 of its 14 known genera (Source: Mugleston et al. 2018, Table 2). Other Hetrodinae genera documented in the literature include Eugaster, Eugasteroides, Hetrodes, Spalacomimus, and Acanthoproctus (e.g. A. diadematus, studied alongside the Acanthoplus congener A. longipes in Namibia) (Source: Grzywacz et al. 2015, Zoologischer Anzeiger 259:2230; Warchaowska-liwa et al. 2015, European Journal of Entomology 112(1)). Cytogenetic studies document a chromosome-number reduction from 29 to 24 (via tandem fusion of acrocentric chromosomes) across Eugaster, Eugasteroides, Hetrodes, and Spalacomimus, and describe independently-derived neo-sex-chromosome systems in two Spalacomimus species sharing 2n=24  proposed as a phylogenetic marker system within Hetrodinae (Source: Grzywacz et al. 2015; Warchaowska-liwa et al. 2015). At the family level, Tettigoniidae comprises more than 7,500 described species across 20 extant subfamilies; five subfamilies (Conocephalinae, Tettigoniinae, Phaneropterinae, Pseudophyllinae, Meconematinae) account for over 85% of described species (Source: Mugleston et al. 2018, citing Cigliano et al. 2017).

technical_sections.heading: 2. Morphology
technical_sections.body: Adults are robust and wide-bodied, roughly 5 cm in body length, coloured brown, green, black, or reddish, with a hard, heavily spined exoskeleton, long antennae, and powerful mandibles capable of a painful bite, suited to tough herbage and carrion feeding (Source: SANBI, Armoured bush cricket). The species is flightless: "ABC is flightless, and although highly mobile for a pedestrian insect, it probably does not move more than a few kilometres in its lifetime" (Source: Green 2002, DFID Report R7428, p.13). Its large body mass  unusual by insect standards  is functionally significant, driving pronounced basking/thermoregulatory behaviour and is implicated as a factor in fecundity (Source: Green 2002, p.42). A 2021 comparative morphometric study of 106 adult A. discoidalis and its congener A. longipes measured body length, pronotal width/length, and hind-leg (femur/tibia) length. Locomotory traits (tibia/femur length) accounted for 99% of the variance separating the two species: A. longipes has a proportionally larger pronotum and hind legs than A. discoidalis, rather than differing in overall body size (Source: Conti, Costa & Mulder 2021, African Entomology 29(1)). The only comprehensive auditory-system study in Hetrodinae (conducted on the congener A. longipes) found a tripartite crista acustica typical of Tettigoniidae, with roughly 27 sensory neurons in the foreleg organ, 18 in the midleg, and 14 in the hindleg. Greatest sensitivity was 410 kHz (threshold 4045 dB SPL), rising to about 60 dB SPL in the ultrasonic range (2040 kHz), with no sexual difference in hearing sensitivity detected (Source: Kowalski & Lakes-Harlan 2010, Journal of Insect Science 10(1):59).

technical_sections.heading: 3. Biology and Life Cycle
technical_sections.body: Females lay tough, porous egg pods containing 612 sibling eggs, 25 cm below the soil surface (Source: Green 2002, DFID Report R7428, pp.6, 9; Mviha, Holt & Green 2022, IJTIS 42:11131121). The egg stage occupies the greatest proportion of the life cycle  roughly 812 months (Source: Green 2002, p.9). Egg diapause follows a complex syndrome: winter-temperature exposure alone (15 C for 30/60/90 days) did not terminate diapause, though prolonged cold delayed hatching by about 10 days per additional 30 days of cold exposure. Incubation temperature strongly affected the proportion of eggs breaking diapause  20 C produced 35% hatch, 25 C produced 55%, and 30 C produced 74% (n=246292 per treatment) (Source: Green 2002, pp.56, Table 1.1). Soil moisture is required only in the later stages of embryonic development; prolonged immersion is lethal (over two weeks kills more than 60% of eggs, three weeks is fatal in almost all cases), while dry-stored eggs can still hatch once moistened months later, only delayed about three days (Source: Green 2002, pp.67). Females select oviposition sites carefully: they avoid pure sand (preferring clay/sand or loam/sand mixtures, P<0.01), strongly prefer dry soil (moisture content above 5% sharply suppresses egg-laying, P<0.001), and prefer uncompacted over compacted soil (P<0.001). In the field, Acacia scrub is the preferred oviposition habitat over crop fields regardless of soil type, with egg-pod density peaking 0.5 m from the trunk and declining sharply beyond 1.52 m (P<0.01) (Source: Green 2002, pp.1012). Roughly half of all eggs die annually in southeast Botswana, dominantly from predation by the subterranean ant Dorylus helvolus (up to 86% of dead eggs in December surveys); egg parasitism by scelionid wasps of genus Nixonia accounted for only about 1%, with desiccation and fungal rot minor factors. Ant predation was consistently higher in crop fields than in Acacia scrub (mean 69.8% vs 39.0% across six sites) and correlated with finer-textured, higher silt/clay soils (Source: Green 2002, pp.79). Hatching begins as early as October in central/northern Botswana and as late as January in the southwest; nymphs then take about two months (southwest) to three months (central/north) to reach adulthood (Source: Mviha, Holt & Green 2022, IJTIS 42:11131121). Mating involves transfer of a spermatophore  a sperm ampulla plus a nutritive spermatophylax "nuptial gift" that can weigh up to 20% of male body mass and is consumed by the female to support egg production. Males preferentially court virgin females (identifiable by lower body mass), transfer spermatophores to them more quickly, and complete more matings with virgins than non-virgins; a male cannot re-mate until he regrows a spermatophore, while a female must mate before her first clutch but can subsequently mate and oviposit in any order due to sperm storage (Source: male mate-choice studies on Botswana A. discoidalis, cited via ResearchGate listings, full text paywalled). Calling and mating behaviour, studied in the directly comparable congener A. longipes, shows males producing multi-minute calling songs (verses of two pulse types, roughly 3 then 5 impulses), distinct from single-pulse disturbance sounds of about 14 impulses; calling-song frequency peaks near 15 kHz at about 87 dB SPL (measured at 10 cm); females show phonotaxis toward calling males; mating lasts over two hours (Source: Kowalski & Lakes-Harlan 2010, Journal of Insect Science 10(1):59). Temporal patterns of acoustic signals differ between closely related Acanthoplus species, plausibly reinforcing species recognition (Source: Kowalski & Lakes-Harlan 2011, Zoology (Jena) 114:2935).

technical_sections.heading: 4. Ecology
technical_sections.body: A. discoidalis is omnivorous and opportunistically carnivorous: it forages on grasses and cereal panicles, scavenges carrion, and has been recorded preying on other insects and even bird nestlings, locating food via chemical cues detected through antennae and palps. Its congener A. longipes, by contrast, is primarily phytophagous, grazing Acacia leaves (Source: Conti, Costa & Mulder 2021, African Entomology 29(1); Green 2002, DFID Report R7428, p.21). The species inhabits areas of low, thick vegetation in cultivated parts of northeastern Namibia and southeastern Botswana, moving from Acacia scrub (its preferred nymphal habitat) into crop fields around panicle emergence, roughly 5060 days after planting (Source: Mviha, Holt & Green 2022; Green 2002, pp.4243, Fig. 4d). In South Africa it also occupies very dry, sparsely vegetated habitats  Kalahari and Namib desert margins, Succulent and Nama Karoo, and Fynbos  most widespread in Northern Cape Province with smaller populations in Western Cape, Eastern Cape, and Limpopo (Source: CABI Compendium datasheet; SANBI species status assessment). Field population monitoring across vegetation types shows a marked daily activity shift: crickets roost in Acacia scrub overnight and at dawn/dusk, then disperse to forage in grasses and crops through the day, with peak feeding around midday and an early-afternoon lull attributed to heat avoidance. Crickets aggregate on the west side of bushes in late afternoon and the east side in the morning, consistent with active behavioural thermoregulation given their unusually large body mass for an insect (Source: Green 2002, pp.4142, Figs. 4b4c). Dispersal differs by crop system: in a sole sorghum crop, males and females showed no significant difference in mean daily displacement (about 7.38.3 m/day, maxima 2527 m); in a mixed sorghum/cowpea intercrop, males dispersed significantly farther than females (mean 12.66 m vs 3.14 m/day, maximum 44.3 m for males), attributed to males switching from "stand-and-sing" acoustic mate attraction toward active mate-searching in the structurally denser mixed-crop habitat (Source: Green 2002, pp.4344, Tables 4.34.4). The species' primary chemical defense is reflex bleeding (autohaemorrhage): it squirts acrid-smelling haemolymph from seams between the trochanter and coxa of each leg and from beneath the pronotum. In the founding study, roughly 62% of attacks directed at the legs elicited autohaemorrhage, ejecting a mean of 13 22 mg of haemolymph over a mean distance of 43 63 mm. Both sexes may also bite and regurgitate crop contents when attacked, and males (but not females) may stridulate during an attack. The haemolymph was shown to be distasteful to at least two reptile species in feeding trials; the specific repellent compounds are unidentified but hypothesized to be phytotoxins sequestered from host plants (Source: Bateman & Fleming 2009, Journal of Zoology 278(4):342348). A related study of the congener A. speiseri found calling males were more reactive to a simulated predatory approach in daylight than in darkness, and more reactive than silent/cryptic males or females in daylight  interpreted as a risk balance between the benefits of exposed acoustic signalling and predation vigilance (Source: Bateman & Fleming 2013, Journal of Insect Behavior 26:1422). Few natural enemies of adults are documented; Botswana farmers regard Abdim's stork (Ciconia abdimii) as a natural predator of the pest. Egg pods are occasionally destroyed by small mammals (e.g. mongoose) and birds, though this was not systematically quantified alongside ant predation (Source: Green 2002, pp.8, 51). Cannibalism is triggered when dietary salt/protein levels drop, and crickets aggregate around dead or dying conspecifics  though controlled Y-tube bioassays found no chemical attraction to dead crickets or fresh egg pods, suggesting this aggregation is opportunistic rather than chemically mediated (Source: Green 2002, pp.23, 27, 29, Table 3.1).

technical_sections.heading: 5. Distribution and Diversity
technical_sections.body: Confirmed range: Namibia, Botswana, South Africa (most widespread in Northern Cape, with smaller populations in Western Cape, Eastern Cape, and Limpopo), and Zimbabwe (Source: OSF, otus/844211; SANBI species status assessment). Crop-damage reports additionally document the pest in Zambia, Angola, and Malawi (Source: CCARDESA). The South African regional population is assessed as Least Concern, citing broad geographic range and adequate occupancy without evidence of severe fragmentation or decline; habitat destruction is flagged as the main potential threat, and no dedicated conservation programme exists beyond pest-management research around 2003 (Source: SANBI species status assessment, August 2013). A global IUCN Red List assessment also exists (Bazelet & Naskrecki 2014), though it could not be directly retrieved and is cited here only via a secondary reference (Source: Mviha, Holt & Green 2022, reference list). Documented congeners include A. longipes (Charpentier, 1845), a long-legged, arid/semi-arid Acacia-associated species that is primarily phytophagous and used as the model species for Hetrodinae auditory research, and A. speiseri Brancsik, 1896, a grain-crop pest in Zambia with its own oviposition-site-selection and thermal-development literature. The genus contains 16 species in total (Source: SANBI; Conti, Costa & Mulder 2021; Mviha, Holt & Green 2022 reference list). At the subfamily/family level, Hetrodinae is sampled across 4 of its 5 tribes and 4 of its 14 known genera in the most recent comprehensive katydid phylogeny, and is recovered as monophyletic; family Tettigoniidae comprises more than 7,500 species across 20 extant subfamilies worldwide (Source: Mugleston et al. 2018, Table 2 and abstract).

technical_sections.heading: 6. Economic / Ecological Importance
technical_sections.body: A. discoidalis is rated the most damaging cereal-panicle pest in northern Namibia (Source: Leuschner 1995, cited in Mviha, Holt & Green 2022), and the second most serious crop pest in eastern Botswana, behind Quelea birds (Source: Matsaert et al. 2000, cited in same paper; corroborated by farmer survey data in Green 2002, p.36). Documented outbreak losses include an estimated 40% sorghum yield loss in the 1990/91 Botswana outbreak, and an estimated 30% total millet yield loss in the 1993 Namibia outbreak (Source: Bashir et al. 1991; Wohlleber 1996; both cited in Green 2002, p.3). More recent reports cite Namibia yield losses of 1080%, and up to 100% crop loss in Zambia's Siavonga and Sinazongwe districts across sorghum, millet, pumpkins, cowpeas, and cucumbers (Source: CCARDESA). Outbreaks superficially resemble migrant-pest plagues (Quelea, armyworm, desert locust) in their visible scale, despite A. discoidalis being non-migratory and flightless (Source: Mviha, Holt & Green 2022, citing Bazelet & Naskrecki 2014 and Green 2002). Contrary to an older assumption that outbreaks follow a multi-year "egg bank" built up through dry years and released by one wet year, the strongest predictor of an outbreak is a single prior season of average (not extreme) rainfall, which best balances fecundity against egg mortality to build the largest viable egg bank. A rule-based forecasting model built on this logic, validated against 19882002 Botswana outbreak records across three climatic zones, found an outbreak was overall 19 times more likely when the model forecast one than when it did not (Source: Mviha, Holt & Green 2022, IJTIS 42:11131121; Green 2002, pp.1318). Contributing factors to intensifying regional outbreaks include climate change, deforestation, land-use change, and weak early-warning systems (Source: CCARDESA). On the positive side, growing interest in insects as food has led to Acanthoplus spp. being explored as an animal and human food source (Source: Yen 2009, cited in Mviha, Holt & Green 2022); some Botswana farmers who hand-picked crickets fed them to chickens, though washing the dead crickets to remove their defensive chemical exudate may be critical for palatability, and some farmers reported their chickens refused to eat them (Source: Green 2002, p.37). No formal veterinary case-report or toxicology literature specifically documenting canine or livestock poisoning from ingesting A. discoidalis was located despite targeted searching; the only relevant toxicity evidence found is the reptile feeding-repellency data noted above, which is inferential rather than a documented poisoning case series (Source: search coverage note, based on Bateman & Fleming 2009). Locally the species is known as "Setotojane" (Setswana). It became the identity of a multi-year DFID-funded crop-protection research and farmer-outreach programme in Botswana ("Setotojane ABC Project"), including original songs and poetry performed by a farmers' choir, an "ABC control poem," and a national farmers' demonstration day at Shoshong, Botswana (11 April 2002), attended by roughly 200 farmers and 50 extension staff from all regions of Botswana. Some farmers had interpreted major outbreaks as a form of divine punishment, reflecting how poorly understood the pest's ecology was before the research programme (Source: Green 2002, pp.2, 36, 5859).

technical_sections.heading: 7. Control and Management
technical_sections.body: Oral-toxicity screening of eight insecticides (LD50, 	g/g, most to least toxic): Fipronil 0.05; Cyfluthrin 0.52; Imidacloprid 1.24; Cypermethrin 2.30; Chlorpyrifos 4.50; Carbaryl 5.00; Gamma-BHC 20.00; Malathion 21.10 (Source: Green 2002, Table 4.2, p.40). The recommended field bait is carbaryl (85% wettable powder) combined with cereal bran (sorghum, maize, or millet bran are equally palatable) at 3 g/kg, targeting LD90. Carbaryl was chosen over the more toxic fipronil due to cost, availability, and lower environmental persistence  fipronil has a soil half-life of 122128 days and poses a sustained hazard to non-target invertebrates (Source: Green 2002, pp.3841). A baited trench (300 mm deep, 20 cm wide, baited with 2.5 g teaspoons of carbaryl/bran bait at 3 m intervals) retained and killed 93% of crickets over 24 hours; a 500 mm depth gave no additional benefit (94%), while unbaited trenches alone were far less effective (3379% retention depending on depth) (Source: Green 2002, pp.4546, Fig. 4g). A 3 m-wide fipronil barrier strip at field edges, applied at 175 g-ai/ha, sustained over 70% mortality for about two weeks and produced a 65% reduction in cricket numbers under real outbreak conditions despite continuous reinvasion from adjacent scrub (Source: Green 2002, pp.5356). Environmental impact assessment (using the pugnacious ant Anoplolepis custodiens as a bioindicator) found carbaryl-baited trenches and fipronil barrier sprays  both targeted, edge-of-field applications  had only a transient effect on non-target invertebrates, with ant activity recovering within 46 weeks. Broadcast/cover application of fipronil across whole plots, by contrast, caused a severe and long-lasting reduction in all sampled arthropod groups (tenebrionid beetles were locally eliminated), with ant activity failing to recover even after eight months (Source: Green 2002, pp.4952). A prototype tractor-mounted mechanical trench digger (chain-mounted hardened steel scrapers) was built and field-tested at Sebele Research Station, Botswana; a modified plough producing a steep-sided furrow (about 70 from horizontal) reduced field entry by roughly 30% and can be pulled by animal traction, a more accessible option for resource-poor farmers than a tractor-drawn digger (Source: Green 2002, pp.4748). Sorghumcowpea intercropping alters cricket dispersal patterns (see Ecology, above). Simple unbaited trenches are more commonly and successfully used by farmers in sandy-soil areas where digging is easier; traditional farmer practices  hand-picking, clean weeding, ritual practices, wire fencing  were widely viewed by farmers themselves as ineffective (Source: Green 2002, pp.3638, 44). Bioassays identified sorghum-panicle volatiles that attract A. discoidalis, including 2-phenylethanol, benzyl alcohol, decanal, and 4-ethylacetophenone; no attraction was found to cricket-derived cues (dead crickets, egg pods), ruling these out as bait attractants. Two octadienone isomers that spike at the soft-dough grain stage were flagged as priority compounds for future attractant development, given their known role as gregarization/pheromone signals in the desert locust Schistocerca gregaria (Source: Green 2002, pp.2128). After a live demonstration of the baited-trench method in 2002, 94% of 60 farmers interviewed said they would adopt it for the next outbreak, up from only 16% who had heard of the method beforehand; farmers had previously strongly opposed surface-broadcast insecticidal baits over safety concerns for children and livestock (Source: Green 2002, pp.3638). More recently, Zambia's Ministry of Agriculture and CABI have developed a mobile-based pest-mapping/forecasting system now being scaled regionally with CCARDESA support under the World Bank-funded Food Systems Resilience Programme; recommended regional integrated pest management measures include intercropping, vegetation buffers, biopesticide exploration, and farmer-led community surveillance and scouting (Source: CCARDESA). The rainfall-based outbreak-forecasting model described under Economic Importance is proposed as an early-warning tool so farmers and extension services can pre-position trenching and baiting responses ahead of a forecast outbreak (Source: Mviha, Holt & Green 2022).

technical_sections.heading: 8. Collection Methods
technical_sections.body:
Coverage here is thin in the authoritative literature reviewed  no dedicated entomological collecting or voucher-specimen protocol paper for A. discoidalis was found. Methods documented are all incidental to ecological and pest-management fieldwork: baited and unbaited trenches, originally designed as control measures, also served as passive population-sampling devices in field trials (Source: Green 2002, pp.4546). Population density monitoring used replicated 4
25 m fixed vegetation-type plots censused repeatedly through a growing season (Source: Green 2002, pp.4143). Markrecapture studies used individually tagged males and females (reflective tags), resighted at night with a spotlight to measure dispersal distances (Source: Green 2002, pp.4344). Egg-pod sampling involved hand excavation of soil to 25 cm depth beneath Acacia bushes and in crop fields, followed by pod counting and laboratory incubation (Source: Green 2002, pp.712). Non-target invertebrate community sampling, for environmental-impact assessment, used pitfall traps, sweep netting, and light traps (Source: Green 2002, p.49).

technical_sections.heading: 9. Notable Facts
technical_sections.body: Reflex bleeding (autohaemorrhage) in A. discoidalis has been shown to be a precisely regulated, targeted defense response rather than an incidental consequence of injury  one of the best-documented examples of this behaviour in Orthoptera (Source: Bateman & Fleming 2009, Journal of Zoology 278(4):342348). Its full defensive repertoire is unusually multi-modal for a single insect: biting, crop-content regurgitation, male-only defensive stridulation, and reflex bleeding of acrid, reptile-repellent haemolymph, layered on top of aposematic coloration and heavy pronotal armor (Source: same; Green 2002). Although outbreaks superficially resemble locust, armyworm, or Quelea-bird plagues in visible scale, A. discoidalis is completely flightless and non-migratory  its "outbreaks" are strictly local phenomena driven by rainfall-modulated egg-bank dynamics rather than mass movement (Source: Mviha, Holt & Green 2022, IJTIS 42:11131121). Roughly 812 months of the animal's life cycle is spent underground in the egg stage  the dominant life-history phase  with diapause termination and hatching tightly gated by soil-moisture and temperature windows (Source: Green 2002, DFID Report R7428, p.9). A striking chemical-ecology parallel: the two octadienone isomers that spike in sorghum-panicle volatiles at the soft-dough stage, and which attract A. discoidalis, are the same compounds known to function as gregarization/maternal-transfer releaser-primer pheromone signals in the desert locust Schistocerca gregaria  raising the possibility of convergent chemical ecology between two very different pest Orthoptera (Source: Green 2002, pp.2526, citing Torto et al. 1999 and Cosse & Baker 1999). Locally known as "Setotojane" in Setswana, the species became the identity and mascot of a multi-year DFID crop-protection research and farmer-outreach programme in Botswana, complete with original songs, poetry, and a national farmers' demonstration day (Source: Green 2002, pp.5859).

sections.heading: What Is It, Really?
sections.body: The spider belongs to the genus Leucauge, nicknamed 'orchard orbweavers,' 'stretch spiders,' or 'long-jawed orb weavers,' with more than 160 species across the tropics and subtropics and at least nine species in Kenya. The exact species in a given photo cannot be confirmed since Leucauge species are usually told apart by microscopic genital structures; the best guess based on coloring is often Leucauge festiva, though this remains an educated guess rather than a certainty.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: The body is oval and elongated with a silvery-white abdomen (from microscopic guanine crystals in the skin), dark stripes, and a splash of reddish-orange near the front, with pale, thin, disproportionately long legs. It rests with its front two leg pairs stretched forward and its back pair stretched behind in a dramatic 'X' pose that, combined with its shape, camouflages it as a twig or blade of grass.

sections.heading: How Do They Live?
sections.body: Leucauge spiders molt while hanging from the center of their own web, often leaving the discarded shell tangled in the silk afterward. Courtship involves the male tapping, jerking, rocking, and twanging the web's silk in a specific sequence; a receptive female responds by opening and closing her fangs and tilting upward. Certain parasitic wasps sting a Leucauge spider and somehow induce it to build a simplified web to hold a wasp cocoon before killing it.

sections.heading: Where Do They Live — and Are They in Kenya?
sections.body: Yes, confidently: a major survey backed by the National Museums of Kenya and international partners documented over 800 spider species in Kenya, nine of them Leucauge. Leucauge festiva specifically is recorded from Nairobi and Moyale and across a wide swath of Africa from Ethiopia and Sudan to South Africa and Madagascar. Checking citizen-recorded iNaturalist sightings, scientists found some Kenyan Leucauge identifications didn't make biological sense — likely misidentifications.

sections.heading: Should You Worry About a Bite?
sections.body: No — long-jawed orbweavers like Leucauge have jaws built for grabbing prey, though their venom is not considered dangerous to people. Of the spiders that do pose a medical risk to humans (widow and recluse spiders), Leucauge isn't among them.

sections.heading: Friend of the Farmer — Sort Of
sections.body: Leucauge eats mosquitoes and other small flies caught in its web, generally acting as a farm ally. However, in Japanese greenhouse eggplant farms, a relative, Leucauge blanda, was found eating a beneficial predatory bug farmers had released to control whiteflies and aphids, since the spider can't distinguish 'good' from 'bad' prey caught in its web.

sections.heading: The Real Marvel: Weaving Together
sections.body: An individual Leucauge web is modest — roughly dinner-plate sized up to about a metre — built from strong 'dragline' silk for the frame and stretchier, gluey silk for the spiral, with some spiders rebuilding up to 90% of the web daily. Some Leucauge species build colonially, with individual webs stitched onto one shared silk scaffold over streams, larger spiders claiming the top spots; others build their webs into the framework of a much bigger Nephila (golden silk orb-weaver) web to save silk.

technical_sections.heading: Identification Note
technical_sections.body: The specimen photographed in Kenya was flagged for identification as an "orchard orbweaver." Genus-level identification as Leucauge (family Tetragnathidae) is confirmed with high confidence: the green/gold cephalothorax with dark longitudinal stripes, reddish mark near the chelicerae, pale slender legs held in the characteristic front-two-pairs-forward/rear-pair-back "X-splay" resting posture, elongated silvery abdomen, and fine-meshed orb web all match the diagnostic description of the genus (Source: Orchard Orbweaver, Orchard Spider Leucauge argyrobapta / Leucauge venusta, UF/IFAS EDIS EENY-728/IN1243, Hall & Rhodes, 2023). Species-level identification is narrowed but not certain. A peer-reviewed checklist of Kenyan spiders lists nine Leucauge species recorded in Kenya: L. amanica, L. brevitibialis, L. camelina, L. festiva, L. kibonotensis, L. levanderi, L. medjensis, L. meruensis, and L. ungulata (Source: Checklist of the spiders (Araneae) of Kenya, African Invertebrates 62(1), Kioko, Marusik, Li, Kioko & Ji, 2021). Of these, Leucauge festiva (Blackwall, 1866) is the strongest single candidate — it is independently confirmed present in Kenya by the World Spider Catalog, the Kioko et al. Kenya checklist, and iNaturalist occurrence records, and its documented coloration ("abdomen silvery, decorated with a reddish mask with hints of maroon, yellow, gold and green" over a "shiny yellow-brown" carapace) closely matches the photographed animal (Source: Notes on the silver vlei spider Leucauge festiva from South Africa, SANSA Newsletter 40, Dippenaar-Schoeman, Jones & Haddad, 2021). However, definitive species diagnosis in Leucauge requires examination of genitalic characters that cannot be assessed from a photograph, so the other eight Kenyan species cannot be fully excluded. Working identification used throughout this summary: genus Leucauge confirmed; species probably L. festiva, unconfirmed. A further nuance: no whitelisted source documents "orchard orbweaver" as a vernacular name for any African Leucauge. That common name is documented specifically for the New World species L. venusta and L. argyrobapta in Florida/southeastern-US literature; the African species (including L. festiva) instead carries the documented South African common name "silver vlei spider" / "masked vlei spider." The "orchard orbweaver" label as applied to this Kenyan specimen is therefore a borrowed genus-level nickname rather than a locally documented common name (Source: UF/IFAS EDIS EENY-728/IN1243, 2023; SANSA Newsletter 40, 2021).

technical_sections.heading: 1. Taxonomy and Classification
technical_sections.body: Order Araneae; family Tetragnathidae Menge, 1866; subfamily Leucauginae (Caporiacco, 1955) (Source: World Spider Catalog, genus record, wsc.nmbe.ch/genus/3286; Checklist of the spiders (Araneae) of Kenya, African Invertebrates 62(1), Kioko et al., 2021). Genus Leucauge White, 1841, originally described as a subgenus of Linyphia; gender feminine; type species Leucauge argyrobapta White, 1841 (Source: World Spider Catalog, genus record, 2024–2025 data). Several genera have been synonymized into Leucauge, including Alcimosphenus, Argyroepeira, Callinethis, Chrysaster, Mecynometa, Opadometa, and Plesiometa Archer — the last synonymy is notable because classic ecological literature on wasp-manipulated webs under the name "Plesiometa argyra" refers to the same species now placed in Leucauge argyra (Source: World Spider Catalog, genus record). The genus is pantropical, with well over 160 described species — one indexed count places the total at 174 species and 8 subspecies (Source: World Spider Catalog, genus and genus-catalog pages). Molecular work using DNA barcoding elevated L. argyrobapta out of junior synonymy with L. venusta, restricting true L. venusta to temperate North American populations while L. argyrobapta covers Florida-to-Brazil populations (Source: cited in UF/IFAS EDIS EENY-728/IN1243, referencing Ballesteros & Hormiga, 2018). Family in Kenya: Tetragnathidae comprises 5 genera and 22 species in Kenya (2.84% of the national spider fauna), with 2 endemic and 13 sub-endemic species. The genera present are Leucauge (9 species), Tetragnatha (6 species), Pachygnatha (4 species), Metellina (2 species), and Sancus (1 species) (Source: Checklist of the spiders (Araneae) of Kenya, African Invertebrates 62(1), Kioko et al., 2021).

technical_sections.heading: 2. Morphology
technical_sections.body: General Leucauge body plan: an oval, elongated abdomen bearing a double row of trichobothria (vibration-sensitive bristles) on the hind legs; legs green to greenish-black with black joints; a tan cephalothorax; a silvery-white abdomen (the silvery sheen produced by thin, platelet-like guanine crystals) marked with dark mid-dorsal and dorsolateral lines running nearly the full body length; and reddish-orange markings — a transverse band in males, a triangular ventral patch in females — that are sometimes mistaken for black-widow markings by the untrained eye (Source: UF/IFAS EDIS EENY-728/IN1243, Hall & Rhodes, 2023). Sexual dimorphism is pronounced: males measure roughly 3.5–4.0 mm in body length, with proportionally longer legs and conspicuous bulbous palpi used in mating; females are larger, at 5.5–7.5 mm, with smaller palpi (Source: UF/IFAS EDIS EENY-728/IN1243). For the African species most plausibly matching the Kenyan specimen, Leucauge festiva: body length 8–9 mm, males smaller than females; carapace shiny yellow-brown, rounded and slightly convex; four median eyes arranged nearly in a square; chelicerae short and thick, bearing strong projecting spurs that are greatly enlarged in males; abdomen silvery with a reddish "mask" showing hints of maroon, yellow, gold and green, plus distinct black spots at the anterior and posterior ends; legs yellowish-brown, long and slender, bearing three claws and numerous spines (Source: Notes on the silver vlei spider Leucauge festiva, SANSA Newsletter 40, Dippenaar-Schoeman, Jones & Haddad, 2021). The characteristic resting posture — two front leg pairs stretched forward, the rear pair stretched backward, forming an X-shape along the body's axis — has earned long-jawed orbweavers the nickname "stretch spiders"; combined with the elongated body, it helps them mimic a twig for camouflage. The family's common name "long-jawed orb weaver" comes from the enlarged, weapon-like chelicerae visible in this posture (Source: Missouri Department of Conservation, "Longjawed Orbweavers" field guide; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, "Spiders," E-408, Brown & Merchant, 2012).

technical_sections.heading: 3. Biology and Life Cycle
technical_sections.body: Egg sacs of L. venusta are built from fluffy orange-white silk, roughly 8–9 mm in diameter, and contain several hundred reddish-orange eggs about 0.4 mm in diameter, commonly attached to a leaf or twig near the edge of the web (Source: UF/IFAS EDIS EENY-728/IN1243, citing Levi, 1980). Orchard orbweavers molt while hanging from the hub of the web, and the shed exoskeleton (exuviae) often remains caught in the web for a period afterward (Source: UF/IFAS EDIS EENY-728/IN1243). Courtship has been studied in detail in the Neotropical congener Leucauge mariana: on entering a female's web, a male performs a distinctive vibratory sequence — rapid jerks of the anterior legs, rhythmic rocking using the fourth leg pair, abdomen bobbing, palp rubbing, twanging of web strands with the third leg pair, and line-tapping with the first and second leg pairs. A receptive female faces downward, repeatedly opens and closes her chelicerae, and bends her abdomen upward; cheliceral clasping by the male precedes copulation (Source: Hairy kisses: tactile cheliceral courtship affects female mating decisions in Leucauge mariana, Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology 69(2), Aisenberg, Barrantes & Eberhard, 2014). Both sexes of L. mariana contribute material to genital "mating plugs" that often occlude the female's genital openings after copulation, a mechanism implicated in cryptic female choice; sexual cannibalism has also been documented in this species (Source: Mating plugs and sexual cannibalism in the Colombian orb-web spider Leucauge mariana, Ethology, Hernández et al., 2018). No lifespan data for any Leucauge species were found in any whitelisted source — this is reported as a genuine gap.

technical_sections.heading: 4. Ecology
technical_sections.body: Leucauge catches small insects across several orders, most commonly small flies (Diptera) including mosquitoes such as Aedes albopictus. Captured prey is crushed and chewed externally by the endites, chelicerae, and fangs; digestive enzymes are pumped onto the prey to liquefy its tissues, and the resulting fluid is drawn into the spider's stomach by alternating muscle contraction, with hairs on the endites and chelicerae straining out solid particles (Source: UF/IFAS EDIS EENY-728/IN1243). Despite the "orchard" name, orchards are only one habitat among several. L. venusta/L. argyrobapta are described as among the most common spiders in Florida citrus groves, but more typically occupy shrubby meadows, woodland edges, wooded suburban areas, and gaps between hedges and buildings under eaves (Source: UF/IFAS EDIS EENY-728/IN1243). Leucauge festiva in South Africa favors orb webs "near water or in shaded damp areas," and is active by day, hanging head-down in its web (Source: SANSA Newsletter 40, Dippenaar-Schoeman, Jones & Haddad, 2021). Documented natural enemies include: •  Mud-dauber wasps (Trypoxylon lactitarse, Sceliphron caementarium), which occasionally provision their nests with Leucauge as prey (Source: UF/IFAS EDIS EENY-728/IN1243). •  Rhomphaea spiders (Theridiidae), which invade Leucauge webs and consume the resident spider directly, using reduced cheliceral teeth to puncture and suck out digested fluid, leaving an empty exoskeleton behind; Leucauge's defense is to drop from the web on a dragline and climb back up later (Source: UF/IFAS EDIS EENY-728/IN1243). •  Ichneumonid ("Darwin") wasp ectoparasitoids of the subfamily Polysphinctinae/Pimplinae, which manipulate host Leucauge behavior dramatically, forcing construction of a simplified "cocoon web" lacking a capture spiral, with radii converging on the hub, that shelters the wasp's cocoon after it kills the spider. Documented cases include Hymenoepimecis pinheirensis on Leucauge volupis (Source: Neotropical Entomology, Almeida, Kloss, Pádua & Gonzaga, 2022) and Hymenoepimecis castilloi on Leucauge mariana in the Colombian Andes at 2,583 m elevation — the first record of this host-parasitoid interaction at high altitude, with modified webs lacking adhesive spirals and anchored by multiple extra threads (Source: Neotropical Entomology, Velasco-Cárdenas, Jacome-García, Pádua & Kloss, 2024). Colonial/social organization has been documented in an undescribed Neotropical Leucauge sp.: colonies of many individual orb webs, joined by a shared scaffolding of communal silk support lines, with each spider holding a private orb-web territory within the shared structure. A size-dependent vertical stratification occurs, with the largest spiders occupying the highest positions in the colony, followed by medium, then extra-small, then small individuals, consistently across colony sizes. Individuals capture and consume prey autonomously and defend their own web territory (Source: Social organization of the colonial spider Leucauge sp. in the Neotropics, Journal of Arachnology 38(3), Salomon, Sponarski, Larocque & Avilés, 2010). Gap noted: whether Argyrodes kleptoparasites (Theridiidae), well documented as web-associates and prey-thieves on Nephila orb webs within the broader Tetragnathidae-adjacent literature (Source: Spider webs as habitat patches: the distribution of kleptoparasites (Argyrodes) among host webs (Nephila, Tetragnathidae), Journal of Arachnology 31(3)), commonly parasitize Leucauge webs specifically could not be confirmed from any whitelisted source.

technical_sections.heading: 5. Distribution and Diversity
technical_sections.body: Leucauge is a pantropical genus with well over 160 described species (one recent count: 174 species and 8 subspecies) (Source: World Spider Catalog, genus and genus-catalog pages). Kenya: A peer-reviewed checklist of Kenyan spiders — authored by researchers affiliated with the Institute of Zoology (Chinese Academy of Sciences), the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, the Institute for Biological Problems of the North (RAS), the National Museums of Kenya, the University of the Free State, and the University of Turku — documents 805 spider species/subspecies across 57 families in Kenya (records to 31 December 2018), of which 300 are Kenya-endemic and 158 sub-endemic. Within this, Tetragnathidae contributes 5 genera and 22 species, of which nine belong to Leucauge: L. amanica Strand 1907 (Mau, Nyandarua County; East Africa), L. brevitibialis Tullgren 1910 (Nairobi, Mau Range; Kenya/Tanzania), L. camelina di Caporiacco 1940 (Mau; Ethiopia/Kenya), L. festiva (Blackwall 1866) (Moyale, Nairobi; pan-African, not endemic/sub-endemic), L. kibonotensis Tullgren 1910 (Mau, Nairobi; Kenya/Tanzania), L. levanderi (Kulczyński 1901) (Elmenteita, Kabete, Nairobi; Ethiopia/DR Congo/Kenya/South Africa), L. medjensis de Lessert 1930 (Mackinnon Road, Nairobi; DR Congo/Kenya), L. meruensis Tullgren 1910 (Mau; Kenya/Tanzania), and L. ungulata (Karsch 1879) (Taru; West & East Africa, Equatorial Guinea, São Tomé and Príncipe) (Source: Checklist of the spiders (Araneae) of Kenya, African Invertebrates 62(1):47–229, Kioko, Marusik, Li, Kioko & Ji, 2021). Cross-checking against the World Spider Catalog's own species distribution record, L. festiva is independently listed with an explicit Kenya distribution ("Ethiopia, Sudan, Kenya, Tanzania, Equatorial Africa, Namibia, South Africa, Eswatini, Madagascar"), making it the most robustly cross-confirmed Kenyan Leucauge species across two independent authorities (Source: World Spider Catalog, species record for Leucauge festiva). iNaturalist occurrence queries for genus Leucauge in Kenya returned 191 observations, with species-level community identifications distributed across L. auronotum (49), L. medjensis (32), L. levanderi (14), L. festiva (2), L. argyrescens (2), L. decorata (1), and L. venusta (1). Cross-checked against the peer-reviewed checklist and World Spider Catalog, the L. medjensis, L. levanderi, and L. festiva identifications corroborate well, but L. auronotum (listed by the World Spider Catalog as South-Africa-endemic) and L. venusta (a Nearctic/Neotropical species with no documented African range) are very likely misidentifications by observers and are not treated as confirmed Kenyan occurrences — illustrating why iNaturalist data is used here only for occurrence corroboration, cross-checked against taxonomic authorities, rather than accepted as biology fact on its own (Source: iNaturalist occurrence data for genus Leucauge, Kenya, cross-checked against World Spider Catalog and Kioko et al., 2021). No Swahili or other Kenyan/East African vernacular name for Leucauge or Tetragnathidae generally was found in any whitelisted source — reported as a genuine gap.

technical_sections.heading: (a) Venom and medical significance to humans
technical_sections.body: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension states explicitly for the family: "The long-jawed spider, in the family Tetragnathidae, is another common orbweaving spider... Their long jaws allow them to bite and secure their prey, though their venom is not considered dangerous to people." The same document notes that in Texas only two spider groups — recluse spiders (Loxosceles) and widow spiders (Latrodectus) — are considered medically significant, with orb-weavers generally, including Tetragnathidae, explicitly excluded from that category (Source: Spiders, E-408, Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, Brown & Merchant, 2012). Notably, the most detailed species-level account available, the UF/IFAS EDIS profile on Leucauge argyrobapta/venusta, contains no discussion at all of venom potency or bite risk to humans — an absence worth reporting honestly rather than filling with inference (Source: UF/IFAS EDIS EENY-728/IN1243). At the family level (in the related genus Tetragnatha, not Leucauge itself), striking sexual dimorphism has been documented in venom chemistry, with males possessing high-molecular-weight venom components absent in females — a pattern not easily explained by dietary or feeding-ecology differences between the sexes, and hypothesized instead to relate to mating biology (Source: Sexual dimorphism in venom chemistry in Tetragnatha spiders is not easily explained by adult niche differences, Toxicon 114, Binford, Gillespie & Maddison, 2016). Assessment: Whitelisted sources that directly address the question (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension) are unambiguous that Tetragnathidae venom is not medically significant to humans. Species-specific data for Leucauge is thin — absent even in the most detailed available species account — so the finding is reported as "not medically significant at the family level, per one solid extension-service source, with a genuine gap at the species level," rather than overstated as a firm species-specific conclusion.

technical_sections.heading: (b) Importance in pest control / biocontrol
technical_sections.body: Spiders in general "are largely beneficial and help keep pests like flies and plant-feeding insects under control," and are noted as generalist predators whose ecological diversity makes them useful for biological control, tolerating conventional pesticides better than many insect pests (Source: Spiders, E-408, Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, 2012). Leucauge's documented predation on small Diptera, including mosquitoes, is consistent with this general role (Source: UF/IFAS EDIS EENY-728/IN1243). Important complicating finding: Leucauge is not purely beneficial from an integrated-pest-management standpoint. A DNA-based study (using PCR primers targeting a 148-bp fragment of mitochondrial COI) confirmed that Leucauge blanda preys heavily on Nesidiocoris tenuis, a mirid bug deliberately released as a biological control agent against whiteflies, aphids, and thrips in Japanese greenhouse eggplant crops — this intraguild predation was cited as a factor complicating recovery of N. tenuis stock for reuse late in production cycles as spider populations built up (Source: Predation of a biological control agent, Nesidiocoris tenuis, by the spider Leucauge blanda in greenhouse eggplant crops, Biocontrol Science and Technology 28(9)). Assessment: No whitelisted source demonstrates a documented pest-control/biocontrol value of Leucauge in an actual orchard setting, nor in Kenyan or wider African agriculture specifically. The "orchard" in the common name reflects habitat association in Florida citrus groves, not a documented agricultural-pest-suppression role. The one well-documented quantitative study available shows Leucauge can act as an intraguild predator consuming a deployed biocontrol agent rather than purely acting as a pest-suppressor — a genuinely double-edged finding that should not be flattened into a simple "beneficial predator" narrative.

technical_sections.heading: 7. Control and Management
technical_sections.body: No whitelisted source discusses control or management measures targeting Leucauge or Tetragnathidae specifically. The only related material is general household spider management guidance (sanitation, exclusion, vacuuming, pyrethroid treatments for medically significant genera) from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, which explicitly does not recommend or discuss any control need for long-jawed orbweavers, consistent with their harmless status (Source: Spiders, E-408, Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, 2012). This topic is thin/effectively absent for the target taxon, which is expected given its lack of pest status.

technical_sections.heading: 8. Collection Methods
technical_sections.body: No whitelisted source describing collection methods specific to Leucauge or Tetragnathidae was found. This topic is reported as a full gap.

technical_sections.heading: 9. Notable Facts
technical_sections.body: Orb web construction: A spider first establishes a bridge line by drifting sticky silk on the wind until it catches a second support; after reinforcing the bridge, it uses its own weight and silk elasticity to form an initial triangle, then adds radii over repeated trips to build the scaffold, before spinning the trademark concentric capture spiral. Orb-weavers use up to seven different silk types in building a web, and many species tear down and recycle up to 90% of the web material daily, rebuilding each morning (Source: Spiders, E-408, Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, 2012). Silk types and mechanics (family/order-general): major ampullate ("dragline") silk forms the structural frame and radii and has tensile strength comparable to steel; flagelliform silk forms the elastic capture spiral, stretching to roughly three times its length before breaking, at about half the tensile strength of dragline silk; piriform silk bonds and anchors threads; aciniform silk wraps prey. Quantitative motion-tracking of the related orb-weaver Uloborus diversus found that spiders follow straight paths while laying radii but orbit around the web center while laying spirals, with a hidden Markov model showing that web-building proceeds through stereotyped, largely shared action sequences across individuals regardless of whether construction follows a "typical" or "atypical" order (Source: Distinct movement patterns generate stages of spider web building, Current Biology, Corver, Wilkerson, Miller & Gordus, 2021). In a related orb-weaving species, Argiope trifasciata (family Araneidae), piriform silk — previously known mainly for anchoring bridging lines to the substrate — was found more abundant in the inner, later-built region of the web where capture-spiral/radial-line junctions are densest, suggesting it also reinforces those junctions against the impact of struggling prey; aggregate glue-protein abundance was found to decline toward web completion, consistent with the spider "running out" of glue material as building progresses (Source: Proteomics suggest pyriform silk attaches orb web capture spiral junctions, Journal of Arachnology 53(2), Lazo, Luzaran, Magoti, Friend, Opell & Ayoub, 2025). Large communal/aggregated web formations — the phenomenon behind claims of unusually wide webs in this family: whitelisted sources do not support single Leucauge orb webs spanning metres; individual webs are on the order of tens of centimetres to about a metre across. What is robustly documented instead is that Leucauge (and the related genus Tetragnatha) achieve the appearance of large-scale, complex web structures through aggregation, in two documented forms: 1.  Colonial clustering: an undescribed Neotropical Leucauge sp. builds colonies of many individual orb webs (each up to roughly a metre in diameter), joined together by a shared scaffolding of communal silk support lines, typically spun over turbulent riparian water, with size-based vertical stratification of individuals within the colony (Source: Social organization of the colonial spider Leucauge sp. in the Neotropics, Journal of Arachnology 38(3), Salomon, Sponarski, Larocque & Avilés, 2010). 2.  Opportunistic aggregation around a larger host spider's web: Leucauge venusta individuals aggregate around the webs of the much larger orb-weaver Nephila clavipes, building their own webs higher and more vertically than usual and omitting their normal barrier web — thereby saving silk by reusing Nephila's anchor threads (Source: Interspecific aggregation around the web of the orb spider Nephila clavipes: consequences for the web architecture of Leucauge venusta, Ethology Ecology & Evolution 22(2), Hénaut & Machkour-M'Rabet, 2010). Separately, in the sister genus Tetragnatha (same family, Tetragnathidae), genuinely large communal "super-webs" have been documented, most commonly near water where flying-insect food sources such as midges are abundant — illustrated by a well-known August 2007 event at Lake Tawakoni State Park, Texas, where a giant communal web was found spanning a large area of shoreline trees, described in the source as "rare for Texas" (Source: Spiders, E-408, Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, 2012). Verdict on "wide/ingenious webs" framing: the ingenuity in this genus lies not in any single spider spinning an unusually large web, but in social/aggregative behavior — colonial webs joined by shared silk scaffolding, or opportunistic piggy-backing on a larger spider's structure — that lets many individual, modest-sized orb webs collectively span a much wider area than any one spider could weave alone.

sections.heading: What Is It?
sections.body: The white-ringed atlas moth is an African emperor moth in the silkmoth family Saturniidae — not a true Attacus atlas moth, which lives only in Asia. Its scientific name, Epiphora mythimnia, was coined in 1849, before the genus Epiphora itself even existed; the moth that later gave that genus its name turned out to be this exact species under a different label. Its closest genetic relatives, oddly, live in Asia and North America rather than Africa, hinting the whole African lineage may descend from a single ancient long-distance crossing.

sections.heading: What Does It Look Like?
sections.body: Despite 175 years of scientific attention, no rigorous published measurement of its wingspan or wing pattern could be found. What is documented is a family trait: an eyespot near the wingtip detailed enough to mimic a vertebrate eye, likely giving a hungry bird pause — probably the source of the 'ringed' in its name, though no source confirms that link directly. The moth's broad, feathery, comb-like antennae (as opposed to a female's slimmer, thread-like ones) mark it out as male, tuned to detect a female's scent from miles away.

sections.heading: How Does It Live?
sections.body: Its basic biology — egg counts, moult stages, time in the cocoon, generations per year — has never been rigorously documented, a striking gap for a species named in 1849. What is confirmed is its diet: caterpillars feed mainly on jujube-type trees in the buckthorn genus Ziziphus, with occasional use of croton trees and one flowering-tree genus, Fernandoa — three of the confirmed feeding records specifically from East Africa.

sections.heading: Where Does It Live, and What Does It Eat?
sections.body: Global occurrence records place this moth in ten African countries, with South Africa holding the majority of sightings and Kenya running second at 27 confirmed records — spanning Nairobi's highland gardens, Nyeri, the coastal lowlands around Kilifi and Taita Taveta, and semi-arid country near Kibwezi and Kasigau. Its wider genus, Epiphora, holds around 20 species, all found only in Africa.

sections.heading: Why Does It Matter?
sections.body: A recent Kenyan survey of edible emperor-and-silk moths across 15 farming zones turned up seven species people eat or could harvest commercially — this one wasn't among them. No conservation status has been confirmed either way, so its ecological or economic weight remains, for now, an open question rather than a settled answer.

sections.heading: A Scientific Plot Twist
sections.body: This species was named in 1849 under a description borrowed from an unrelated moth family, then formally rehomed in 1860 into a brand-new genus built around a specimen that turned out to be the very same species under another name — while its true genetic relatives turned up on two continents it has never lived on.

sections.heading: What's the Kenya Connection?
sections.body: Kenya is a genuine, well-documented part of this moth's range, with records running from Nairobi's high-altitude gardens to the hot coastal bush near Kilifi and out into the dry country near Kibwezi — mostly drawn from decades of private and museum lepidopterist collections, plus more recent citizen sightings around Nairobi.
