technical_sections.heading: 1. Taxonomy and Classification
technical_sections.body: •  Order: Coleoptera (Source: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy, api.gbif.org, 2026). •  Family: The genus Brachycerus is currently accepted by GBIF's backbone taxonomy under family Brachyceridae (common name "Lily Weevils," ~622 subordinate names listed) (Source: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy, api.gbif.org/v1/species/1227966, 2026). Individual species records in the same database, including B. ornatus, are still filed under family Curculionidae with taxonomic status flagged "DOUBTFUL" — an unresolved placement visible directly in the live record (Source: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy, api.gbif.org/v1/species/8204693, 2026). •  Subfamily/Tribe: Brachycerus, together with roughly ten smaller related genera, forms the tribe Brachycerini within subfamily Brachycerinae, described as a primitive, largely African weevil element (Source: Oberprieler, Journal of the Entomological Society of Southern Africa, journals.co.za). •  Broader placement: Curculionoidea (the weevil superfamily containing Brachycerinae) is organised into seven main lineages/families (Source: Oberprieler, Marvaldi & Anderson, "Weevils, weevils, weevils everywhere," Zootaxa 1668(1):491–520, 2007). •  Species groups (southern Africa): three main groups are recognised — the B. apterus group (largest; larvae develop in Amaryllidaceae bulbs), the B. asparagi group, and the B. inaequalis group (Source: Oberprieler, journals.co.za). •  Species count: GBIF lists at least 300 accepted species-rank taxa under the genus, with more beyond the first page of records (Source: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy, api.gbif.org/v1/species/1227966/children, 2026). A separate paper on Lebanese Brachycerus fauna states the genus comprises approximately 300 species, mostly in the Ethiopian zoogeographical region, with far fewer (49 species plus two subspecies) in the Palaearctic, primarily North Africa (Source: ResearchGate-hosted paper on Lebanese Brachycerus fauna). •  Genus-level identification of this specimen is well supported; species-level determination could not be confirmed from any whitelisted source using photographic features alone, and is reported as undetermined.

technical_sections.heading: 2. Morphology
technical_sections.body: •  Robust, flightless, black-bodied weevils; Palaearctic representatives in identification keys range roughly 6–18 mm in body length; rostrum dorsally flattened; cuticle surface strongly furrowed and embossed; elytra fused and coarsely sculptured (Source: Digital-Weevil-Determination key for Curculionoidea of the West Palaearctic, Brachycerinae, ResearchGate). •  Antennae are short, compact, non-geniculate (not elbow-shaped, unlike most other weevils), composed of nine segments (Source: same ResearchGate key). •  Species-level diagnostic characters used in keys include: interstriae 3 and 5 more prominently tuberculate than the others; a pronotal medial groove with a strongly prominent longitudinal carina; in some species the outer distal angle of the fore and mid tibiae is strongly prominent and knife-like; at least one described species shows sexual dimorphism in the shape of the apical elytra (Source: same ResearchGate key).

technical_sections.heading: 3. Biology and Life Cycle
technical_sections.body: •  Larvae of the B. apterus species-group develop internally within the bulbs of host Amaryllidaceae, with recorded host genera including Crinum, Ammocharis, Clivia, Cyrtanthus, and Nerine (Source: Oberprieler, journals.co.za). •  No accessible whitelisted source described egg-stage detail, pupation, adult reproductive behaviour, or adult lifespan for this genus; this part of the life cycle is genuinely thin in the available literature rather than omitted for space.

technical_sections.heading: 4. Ecology
technical_sections.body: •  Within southern Africa, the known host plants of the Brachycerini belong to the broader lily-family group that includes the Amaryllidaceae (Source: Oberprieler, journals.co.za). •  Exceptional species richness of large, flightless, aridity-adapted weevil lineages, including Brachycerus, occurs in the Nama Karoo of southern Africa — a region that is otherwise unremarkable for plant diversity — exceeding richness found in the Succulent Karoo and Cape Floristic Region, both recognised plant-diversity hotspots; grassland/savanna of southeastern Africa also shows elevated richness despite non-arid conditions (Source: Hickman, Procheş & Ramdhani, "Patterns of species richness in two African-centered, aridity-adapted flightless weevil lineages," Zootaxa 4323(4), 2017). •  Brachycerus ornatus and its bulb host Boophone disticha (= Ammocharis coranica) feature recurrently in southern African healing (ngoma) traditions across San, Khoe, Bantu-speaking, and settler-descended communities (Source: Thornton, "Magical weevils and amaryllis in southern African ritual landscapes," in Healing the Exposed Being, Wits University Press, 2017). •  No IUCN Red List entries were found for the genus or for any individual Brachycerus species.

technical_sections.heading: 5. Distribution and Diversity
technical_sections.body: •  The genus occurs predominantly in Africa; approximately 300 species are found mostly in the Ethiopian zoogeographical region, with about 49 species and two subspecies in the Palaearctic, primarily North Africa (Source: ResearchGate-hosted paper on Lebanese Brachycerus fauna). •  Kenyan occurrence, confirmed directly via live GBIF occurrence records: •  B. ornatus (Reiche, 1857) — Kajiado/Kitengela, February 2022; Laikipia/Mugogodo West, June 2020 •  B. puerilis (Kolbe, 1898) — Kilifi/Dakatcha Woodland, May 2024 •  B. strumosus (Pascoe, 1887) — Nakuru/Rift Valley, June 1962 •  B. kumbanensis (Quedenfeldt, 1888) — Kakamega, Western Province •  Genus-level museum and citizen-science records from Tsavo East National Park/Kitui (1977–1989) and Kikambala/Kilifi (1977) •  (Source: GBIF occurrence search, api.gbif.org, live query, 2026) •  CABI Compendium distribution data for B. albidentatus (onion weevil) lists a broad range including Angola, Egypt, Ethiopia, Israel, Italy, Jordan, Kenya, Libya, Malta, Senegal, Somalia, South Africa, Tanzania, Turkey, UAE, Yemen, and Zimbabwe (Source: CABI Compendium datasheet 9895, excerpt only). •  By contrast, SANBI's Biodiversity Advisor record for B. oblongus shows only South African occurrence (Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Gauteng, 1895–2014), illustrating that Kenyan range is species-specific within the genus rather than genus-wide (Source: SANBI Biodiversity Advisor, biodiversityadvisor.sanbi.org, record 6545).

technical_sections.heading: 6. Economic / Ecological Importance
technical_sections.body: •  Three Brachycerus species are treated as named agricultural pests in the CABI Compendium: B. albidentatus (onion weevil), B. muricatus (garlic weevil), and B. undatus (garlic weevil) (Source: CABI Compendium datasheets 9895, 9896, 9898, excerpt only). •  A 2023 peer-reviewed survey of emerging soil-dwelling pests of onions and cabbage in Kenya found no mention of Brachycerus at all; the pests identified were Delia platura, Maladera sp., Agriotes sp., Atherigona orientalis, and Urophorus humeralis (Source: Scientific Reports, 2023, PMC10624810). Current published Kenyan pest-surveillance literature accessed for this report does not flag Brachycerus as an economically significant pest within Kenya. •  Ecologically, larvae of at least the B. apterus group act as internal bulb-feeders on wild Amaryllidaceae, a non-crop, wild-plant association rather than a documented Kenyan agricultural one based on sources accessed (Source: Oberprieler, journals.co.za).

technical_sections.heading: 7. Control and Management
technical_sections.body: No authoritative coverage could be obtained for this topic. CABI Compendium datasheets nominally include prevention/control sections for the three named pest species, but full text was inaccessible (403 Forbidden) across every route attempted.

technical_sections.heading: 9. Notable Facts
technical_sections.body: •  Brachycerus ornatus and its host bulb Boophone disticha are documented as recurring elements of southern African ngoma healing traditions spanning multiple ethnic groups over a long historical span (Source: Thornton, Healing the Exposed Being, Wits University Press, 2017). •  For scale, the broader weevil superfamily Curculionoidea, within which Brachycerinae sits, comprises roughly 62,000 described species against an estimated total of 220,000 (Source: Oberprieler, Marvaldi & Anderson, Zootaxa 1668, 2007). •  Large African flightless weevil lineages including Brachycerus reach their greatest species richness in the Nama Karoo, an arid region that is not itself a recognised plant-diversity hotspot — richness there exceeds that of the genuinely plant-diverse Cape Floristic Region and Succulent Karoo (Source: Hickman, Procheş & Ramdhani, Zootaxa 4323(4), 2017). •  GBIF's own current database simultaneously carries the accepted genus record under family Brachyceridae while several individual species, including B. ornatus, remain filed under family Curculionidae with "DOUBTFUL" status — a live, present-day taxonomic inconsistency rather than settled history (Source: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy, api.gbif.org, 2026).

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: These are jewel beetles — a family of over 15,000 species worldwide, famous for wearing what looks like polished metal instead of ordinary insect armour. The beetles in this photo, clustered together feeding on a yellow daisy-like flower, most likely belong to a genus called Meliboeus, which is known to visit flowers for pollen and has confirmed populations in Kenya — though pinning down the exact species from a photo alone isn't possible, so think of this as a strong, evidence-backed guess rather than a certainty.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Adult jewel beetles have a hard, teardrop-shaped body, flattened top to bottom, with short antennae and ridged or grooved wing covers. But the real showstopper is the colour. That shimmering green-blue isn't paint or pigment at all — it's built from dozens of microscopically thin layers in the beetle's outer shell, stacked so precisely that they bend and reflect light the way a soap bubble or an oil slick does. Scientists studying a close relative found around 16 alternating layers producing the green shimmer, packed into a shell just over a thousandth of a millimetre thick. At certain angles the reflected light even becomes polarised — a property invisible to us but possibly used by the beetles themselves to spot a still, silent mate sitting nearby.

sections.heading: How Do They Live?
sections.body: A jewel beetle's life starts as an egg tucked into bark or a plant wound. The larva that hatches is a strange-looking grub with a flattened, oversized "head" segment — entomologists nickname them "flatheaded borers" for exactly that reason — and it tunnels through wood or plant stems as it feeds and grows. Depending on the species, that tunnelling phase can be astonishingly long: one African jewel beetle, Sternocera orissa, is documented taking up to 35 years to finish developing as a larva before finally emerging as a short-lived, flying adult. Adults of many species, though, spend their days doing something much gentler than boring through wood — visiting flowers to feed on pollen and nectar, exactly as this cluster is doing.

sections.heading: Where Do They Live?
sections.body: Jewel beetles turn up across Kenya, from the dry northern counties of Wajir and Marsabit to the highlands around Nairobi and Naivasha, and down into the hot savanna near Kajiado and Taita Taveta. Museum and citizen-science records place several genera — Sternocera, Lampetis, Julodis, and the pollen-loving Meliboeus candidate identified here — right across these very different Kenyan landscapes, from arid scrubland to moist forest edge.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: Beyond their ecological role — some feeding on wood, others visiting flowers — jewel beetles carry real cultural weight in East Africa. Their glittering wing covers are strung into ceremonial necklaces: Maasai and Samburu women wear necklaces made from Sternocera hildebrandti elytra alternated with seeds for special occasions, and the Kamba people of Kenya make similar ornaments. Beyond Africa, jewel beetle wings were once stitched by the thousand onto Victorian gowns as a shimmering, biodegradable alternative to sequins — a fashion trend that started in royal courts in India and spread through the British Empire. Some species are also eaten; one southern African jewel beetle is prized enough as food that a small handful can supply half a day's zinc requirement, and is reported to taste something like eland meat when roasted in hot ash.

sections.heading: Anything Surprising?
sections.body: One relative of these beetles, the aptly-named "fire beetle," can detect a forest fire from over 100 kilometres away using heat-sensing organs on its body — among the most sensitive infrared detectors known in the animal kingdom. It seeks out fires deliberately, because its larvae can only survive in wood that has just been burned. It's a reminder that the same family producing beetles glamorous enough for royal fashion also produced one of nature's most extreme heat-sensing instruments.

technical_sections.heading: 1. Taxonomy and Classification
technical_sections.body: Jewel beetles (also called metallic wood-boring beetles) belong to order Coleoptera, family Buprestidae, superfamily Buprestoidea. The family comprises roughly 15,000 species in 522 genera worldwide (Source: Kelnarova, Jendek, Grebennikov & Bocak, Bulletin of Entomological Research, 2018). Two subfamilies are relevant here. Agrilinae is the largest subfamily, comprising four tribes — Coraebini, Agrilini, Aphanisticini, and Tracheini — with Agrilus (tribe Agrilini) the largest genus in the family at over 3,000 species, and Meliboeus placed in tribe Coraebini (Source: Huang et al., PLoS ONE, 2023). Julodinae comprises a single tribe of six genera, including Julodis and Sternocera, distributed mainly across arid and semi-arid Afrotropical and Palaearctic zones, with Sternocera extending into humid tropical Asia and Africa as an exception to that pattern (Source: Wei, Huang & Shi, ZooKeys, 2023). Species-level identification of the photographed specimens could not be confirmed, but the visible features — small size, elongated body, metallic green-to-blue colouring, and longitudinally ridged elytra, clustered feeding on the disc florets of a yellow composite flower — are consistent with genus Meliboeus at moderate confidence. Two Meliboeus species are confirmed present in Kenya via National Museum of Kenya specimen records: Meliboeus albopilosus and Meliboeus conradsi (Source: GBIF occurrence records, National Museum of Kenya). Supporting this candidate identification, some Meliboeus species are documented as adult pollen-feeders (Source: Huang et al., PLoS ONE, 2023), consistent with the observed flower-clustering behaviour. If the specimens are not Meliboeus, family-level identification as Buprestidae stands as the confirmed conclusion. Other Buprestidae genera confirmed present in Kenya via specimen and observation records include Sternocera, Lampetis, Julodis, Pseudocastalia, and Agrilus (Source: GBIF and iNaturalist occurrence data, National Museum of Kenya specimens).

technical_sections.heading: 2. Morphology
technical_sections.body: Adult jewel beetles are hardened, teardrop-to-bullet-shaped, dorsoventrally flattened beetles with a pronotum roughly as wide as the abdomen, and short, weakly serrate antennae reaching at most the base of the elytra. Larvae — known as "flatheaded borers" — are legless and whitish to yellow, with a greatly enlarged and flattened first thoracic segment behind a tiny head, the character most reliably used to distinguish them from other wood-boring beetle larvae (Source: UC IPM, University of California Statewide IPM Program). The family's characteristic metallic iridescence is a structural colour, produced by multilayer interference reflectors in the epicuticle rather than by pigment. In the jewel beetle Chrysochroa fulgidissima, green cuticle regions contain around 16 alternating-density layers with a roughly 160 nm period, while purple regions have around 12 layers with a roughly 205 nm period; the total reflecting stack is about 1.3 micrometres thick, with melanin providing an absorptive backing. At oblique viewing angles of around 60 degrees, the reflected colour becomes strongly polarised (Source: Stavenga et al., Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 2011). Longitudinal ridging or rows of punctures on the elytra are common across the family; in Sternocera orissa the pronotum and elytra bear white or yellowish patches over a grooved surface pattern, and females are notably larger-bodied than males (Source: Masehela, SANBI, 2015).

technical_sections.heading: 3. Biology and Life Cycle
technical_sections.body: The standard buprestid life cycle runs egg to larva (four instars) to pupa to adult. Mated females lay eggs in bark crevices or wounds; larvae bore into the host and feed in the cambium layer, producing flattened, winding, frass-packed galleries. Mature larvae typically overwinter under bark before pupating, and adults emerge through characteristic D-shaped or oval exit holes. Most species complete one generation per year (Source: UC IPM, University of California Statewide IPM Program). Larval habits vary meaningfully by subfamily: Agrilini and Coraebini larvae (including Meliboeus and Agrilus) bore into wood or plant stems; Aphanisticini and Tracheini larvae are leaf-miners; Julodinae larvae are instead soil-dwelling external root feeders, while Julodinae adults feed on foliage rather than boring wood (Source: Huang et al., PLoS ONE, 2023; Wei, Huang & Shi, ZooKeys, 2023). For Sternocera orissa in southern Africa, females lay eggs from mid-December to late January in bark crevices or soil; larvae are free-living root feeders completing one reproductive cycle per year; adults are comparatively short-lived, but larval development can take up to 35 years. Adults are described as clumsy, reluctant fliers, social and semi-gregarious, spending much time clinging to branches and flowers (Source: Masehela, SANBI, 2015).

technical_sections.heading: 4. Ecology
technical_sections.body: Many Buprestidae adults feed on foliage, pollen, and nectar rather than boring wood themselves — only the larvae bore. Pollen-feeding is specifically documented for some Meliboeus species (Source: Huang et al., PLoS ONE, 2023). Sternocera orissa adults consume foliage and nectar on flowering thorn trees including Vachellia, Senegalia, Dichrostachys cinerea, and Gymnosporia senegalensis, in moist-to-dry savanna, bushveld, and sand-forest habitat, and have been noted competing with honeybees for nectar and pollen (Source: Masehela, SANBI, 2015). In Kenya, Agrilus sp. was recorded as a wood-borer of Acacia xanthophloea (yellow fever tree) at sites in Nairobi and Machakos County, accounting for a minority share of beetles recovered relative to a larger Bostrichidae borer community; predators (Histeridae, Cleridae, Cerambycidae) and parasitoids (Braconidae, Ichneumonidae, Chalcididae) were recovered from the same wood samples (Source: Kahuthia-Gathu et al., PLoS One, 2018).

technical_sections.heading: 5. Distribution and Diversity
technical_sections.body: Globally, Buprestidae comprises roughly 15,000 species in around 522 genera, with greatest diversity in tropical and subtropical regions (Source: Kelnarova, Jendek, Grebennikov & Bocak, Bulletin of Entomological Research, 2018). Confirmed Kenyan occurrence records (National Museum of Kenya specimens and Research-Grade iNaturalist observations) include: Sternocera castanea boucardii (Samburu, Kilifi, Taita Taveta), Sternocera hunteri (Kajiado, Tsavo National Park), Sternocera hildebrandti (Kajiado South), Lampetis lethalis (Laikipia, Karura Forest/Nairobi), Lampetis impressa (Ikutha, Kitui), Pseudocastalia bennigseni (Kirimon, Laikipia), Julodis spp. (Wajir, Marsabit, Emali/Makueni — dryland northeastern and eastern Kenya), Meliboeus albopilosus (Limuru, Naivasha, Kabete/Nairobi, Nakuru, Chyulu Hills), and Meliboeus conradsi (Mwea, Nairobi, Kimilili/Trans Nzoia) (Source: GBIF and iNaturalist occurrence data, National Museum of Kenya). More broadly in Africa, Sternocera orissa ranges across Botswana, Mozambique, Namibia, Malawi, South Africa, Tanzania, and Zambia (Source: Masehela, SANBI, 2015).

technical_sections.heading: 6. Economic / Ecological Importance
technical_sections.body: Buprestidae are recorded as secondary forest and timber pests in Kenya, attacking wood at all stages from log to seasoned wood and finished products, and found in forests, timber depots, sawmills, and furniture industries alongside Bostrichidae and Curculionidae (Source: Kahuthia-Gathu et al., PLoS One, 2018). Elsewhere, most buprestids are secondary pests of already-stressed or damaged trees (Source: UC IPM, University of California Statewide IPM Program). Adults of many species, including Meliboeus, visit flowers for pollen and nectar (Source: Huang et al., PLoS ONE, 2023). The elytra of jewel beetles carry notable cultural and economic value as decoration. Sternocera aequisignata elytra are the traditional material for "beetlewing" embroidery, originating in Mughal India and later adopted into Victorian-era European fashion via East India Company trade, with elytra sewn onto cloth alongside gold-thread zardozi embroidery; production for Western export was centred in Chennai by the mid-19th century (Source: Libes, Fashion History Timeline, FIT; Angus, Cooper Hewitt Smithsonian Design Museum, 2018). Contemporary beetle-elytra decorative use persists among Southeast Asian minority groups. Within Kenya specifically, buprestid elytra are threaded into ceremonial necklaces: Sternocera hildebrandti elytra, alternated with legume seeds, are worn by Maasai and Samburu women during special ceremonies, and elytra ornaments are also documented among the Kamba of Kenya. Commercial trade in prized decorative jewel beetles or their elytra can reach US$20–600 per specimen (Source: van Huis, Insects, 2021). Jewel beetles are also eaten. Sternocera orissa is among the most-consumed insects in South Africa; 10.6 g of adult beetle provides roughly half the recommended daily zinc allowance, and its protein content has been reported to exceed that of fish, pork, or chicken by some measures. San people of the Kalahari roast the beetles in hot ash or sand after removing the wings (Source: Masehela, SANBI, 2015; Lategan, MSc thesis, Stellenbosch University, 2019). Consumption of Sternocera orissa, Sternocera interrupta, Steraspis speciosa, and Psiloptera sp. is documented more broadly across southern Africa, and buprestid eggs are eaten in Mali (Source: van Huis, Insects, 2021). Conservation status is a gap for the family in this region: Sternocera orissa has never been formally IUCN-evaluated and is currently unprotected in South Africa, despite documented overharvesting and habitat-loss pressure from removal of fuelwood and fencing trees (Source: Masehela, SANBI, 2015).

technical_sections.heading: 7. Control and Management
technical_sections.body: No Kenya- or Africa-specific pest-management protocol for Buprestidae was found among whitelisted sources searched. General (non-Kenya) integrated pest management guidance includes: predatory beetle larvae, parasitoid wasps, mites, and woodpeckers as natural enemies of buprestid larvae; maintaining tree vigour through proper irrigation and fertilisation; trunk whitewashing or wrapping to prevent sunscald-driven attack; prompt pruning and destruction of infested material; avoiding pruning during the adult flight season; and solarising cut wood under clear plastic. Where chemical control is used, a spring application of carbaryl or a pyrethroid targeted at egg-laying adults is typical, generally restricted to professional applicators and most effective when combined with monitoring (Source: UC IPM, University of California Statewide IPM Program). No documented case of insecticide resistance in the family was found.

technical_sections.heading: 8. Collection Methods
technical_sections.body: Purple prism or panel traps are the standard method for monitoring adult metallic wood-boring beetle emergence: a corrugated plastic panel painted purple, coated with a sticky adhesive, folded into a triangular prism, and mounted on a stake; traps are deployed ahead of the spring emergence window and checked weekly (Source: NC State Extension Publications, Edwards et al., 2025).

technical_sections.heading: 9. Notable Facts
technical_sections.body: The fire beetle Melanophila acuminata possesses thoracic pit organs, each containing around 70 dome-shaped infrared sensilla, among the most sensitive infrared receptors documented in the animal kingdom. Beetles are drawn to forest fires because larvae can only develop in freshly fire-killed wood; modelling based on a historic 1925 oil-tank fire estimated detection thresholds low enough to sense a fire from up to 130 km away (Source: Schmitz & Bousack, PLoS One, 2012). Sternocera orissa larval development can take up to 35 years, an extreme outlier for insect development time (Source: Masehela, SANBI, 2015). The polarised iridescence of Chrysochroa fulgidissima elytra may function as a visual cue for detecting a stationary conspecific, potentially serving as a mate-recognition signal (Source: Stavenga et al., Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 2011). Jewel beetles carry documented ceremonial significance in Kenya specifically: Maasai and Samburu women's necklaces made from Sternocera hildebrandti elytra alternated with legume seeds, and Kamba elytra ornaments, are direct evidence of this same beetle family's cultural role in the region where these specimens were photographed (Source: van Huis, Insects, 2021).

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Imagine a fly whose eyes sit at the tips of two long rods sticking out sideways from its head — wider, in some species, than the fly's entire body is long. That's a stalk-eyed fly. They belong to the family Diopsidae, a group of around 240 known species worldwide, and Africa is their stronghold: about two-thirds of all described species live here, making a Kenyan encounter with one entirely at home.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: The whole head plan is rearranged around those eyestalks — the eyes and antennae are pushed out to the very ends of diverging rods, rather than sitting flush on the head the way they do in almost every other fly. Not every member of the family goes this far, though: a stalkless subfaimly called the Centrioncinae, found in African montane forests including several Kenyan mountains, keeps its eyes in the ordinary place. Males usually grow noticeably longer eyestalks than females do. Those stalks aren't just decoration — males use them in stand-offs over prized resting spots, sizing each other up before deciding whether to fight, and both sexes appear to size up potential partners by eyestalk length too.

sections.heading: Where Do They Live?
sections.body: Most stalk-eyed flies favour damp places — lake shores, riverbanks, and moist forest — where their larvae feed on rotting plant matter as decomposers. A smaller number of species have taken a different path and become stem-borers: their larvae tunnel into living rice plants instead, which is where the family crosses into farmers' lives. One such species, Diopsis longicornis, is documented across sub-Saharan Africa including Kenya and Tanzania.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: The stem-boring species are a real headache for African rice growers. The larvae burrow down inside the stem toward the growing point, and their feeding dries out the central shoot — a symptom farmers call "dead-heart." Yield losses of 10–15% have been documented where these pests take hold. The good news is that researchers have found some clever, low-chemical ways to fight back. Certain rice varieties actually lure egg-laying females in, only for the variety's own toxicity to kill the larvae once they hatch — a trap crop that does the pest's own instincts against it. Other varieties give off scents that put egg-laying females off entirely. Tiny parasitic wasps that attack the fly's eggs and larvae add another natural line of defence, alongside the more familiar option of insecticide sprays.

sections.heading: Something Worth a Second Look
sections.body: Most Diopsidae are quiet decomposers doing useful, unglamorous work breaking down rotting vegetation — it's only a handful of species that turn to farmers' crops. And scientists still haven't finished cataloguing them: roughly 65 African species with a distinctive wing marking are known to exist but have yet to be formally named and described, meaning a good deal of this family's diversity is still waiting to be written up.

technical_sections.heading: 1. Taxonomy and Classification
technical_sections.body: Class Insecta, Order Diptera, Family Diopsidae, taxonomic status accepted, with 294 descendant taxa recorded (Source: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy, GBIF.org). The family comprises three subfamilies: Diopsinae (the largest), Centrioncinae, and Sphyracephalinae, placed within superfamily Diopsoidea. Approximately 240 described species are recognised in 17 genera, with 66% (157 species) recorded from the Afrotropical region (Source: Insect of the Week: Stalk-Eyed Flies, icipe, 2023). Genus Diopsis Linnaeus, 1775 is the type genus of Diopsinae and is described as very large, requiring comprehensive taxonomic revision; nine provisional species-groups have been proposed, and roughly 65 African species with a large apical wing spot remain undescribed (Source: Feijen & Feijen, African Invertebrates 53(1), 2012). Diopsis phlogodes is a synonym of Diopsis longicornis, a well-known rice stem borer distributed across sub-Saharan Africa including Kenya and Tanzania (Source: Feijen & Feijen, African Invertebrates 53(1), 2012). Subfamily Centrioncinae ("Afromontane Forest Flies") consists of small (4–7 mm), stalkless flies endemic to Africa. Its classification history moved from family Sepsidae (1910) to Diopsidae (1950), briefly to its own family Centrioncidae (1983), and back to a subfamily of Diopsidae following further study. Genus Centrioncus Speiser, 1910 contains 10 recognised species, seven of which occur in Eastern Africa, with Kenyan localities at Mount Elgon, the Kasigau Massif, and the Taita Hills (Source: Feijen & Feijen, ZooKeys 1144, 2023). Given the photographed specimen's long, stalked eyes (not the stalkless condition of Centrioncinae) and the documented Kenyan/East African occurrence of Diopsis longicornis, genus Diopsis is the best-supported assignment from available sources; the exact species could not be confirmed without direct specimen examination of the diagnostic wing-spot pattern.

technical_sections.heading: 2. Morphology
technical_sections.body: The family's diagnostic feature is "the enormous displacement of the eyes along with the antennae from the rest of the head onto the tip of diverging stalks," with stalk length exceeding body length in some species. Centrioncinae is the exception, retaining normally positioned eyes (Source: Insect of the Week, icipe, 2023). The apical wing spot is a key diagnostic character for Diopsis species identification — described as large and rounded brown, with variable shape and extent between species (Source: Feijen & Feijen, African Invertebrates 53(1), 2012). Diopsis longicornis is described as large and robust, with a dorsally pruinose collar and glossy black scutum, and is considered the most important diopsid species affecting agriculture in the region (Source: CABI Compendium, Diopsis longicornis datasheet). Centrioncus species show dark maxillary palps, a central wing spot, incrassate (thickened) fore femora, and distinctive abdominal sclerites (Source: Feijen & Feijen, ZooKeys 1144, 2023). Males typically have longer eyestalks than females, an observed and measurable trait; eyestalks are used by males in visual and physical contests over aggregation sites, and eyestalk length is used by both sexes in mate assessment (Source: Insect of the Week, icipe, 2023).

technical_sections.heading: 3. Biology and Life Cycle
technical_sections.body: Larvae of pest Diopsis species bore into rice stems and move down the leaf sheath toward the meristem, where feeding causes drying of the central shoot (the "dead-heart" symptom) (Source: Bocco et al., Insects 16(8):752, 2025). Diopsis apicalis females select oviposition sites using olfactory cues from rice leaf volatiles. Some rice accessions are strongly attractive for egg-laying while being toxic to developing larvae, and others chemically repel egg-laying females (Source: Bocco et al., Insects 16(8):752, 2025). Males contest ownership of aggregation/roosting sites, with males of larger eyespan winning a greater proportion of these contests and site-owning males securing more matings (Source: search-indexed content of a whitelisted domain covering Diopsidae behavioural studies; direct full-text access was blocked — reported at moderate confidence).

technical_sections.heading: 4. Ecology
technical_sections.body: Diopsids inhabit moist environments such as lake shores and riverine forests. Larvae are primarily saprophagous, feeding on decaying organic matter, though some Diopsis species are phytophagous, boring into living plant tissue such as rice stems (Source: Insect of the Week, icipe, 2023). Diopsis apicalis occurs across all rice ecological zones of tropical Africa but is found preferentially in wet and shady lowland areas and irrigated rice fields (Source: Bocco et al., Insects 16(8):752, 2025). Diopsis longicornis, D. apicalis, and D. collaris use alternative host plants including goosegrass and Johnson grass, sustaining populations outside the rice-growing season (Source: Pegalepo et al., Insects 16(11):1175, 2025).

technical_sections.heading: 5. Distribution and Diversity
technical_sections.body: Diopsidae comprises around 240 described species in 17 genera worldwide; 66% are Afrotropical, and the family is most diverse in the Afrotropical and Oriental regions while absent from the Neotropics. Centrioncinae is endemic to Africa (Source: Insect of the Week, icipe, 2023). Diopsis longicornis is distributed across sub-Saharan Africa, including Kenya and Tanzania (Source: Feijen & Feijen, African Invertebrates 53(1), 2012; corroborated by CABI Compendium). Diopsis apicalis is documented predominantly in West and Central Africa (Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Chad, Gabon, Gambia, Ghana, Ivory Coast, Liberia, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Togo), a more westerly range than D. longicornis (Source: CABI Compendium, Diopsis apicalis datasheet). Kenyan Centrioncinae occurrences (a stalkless subfamily of Diopsidae) are documented at Mount Elgon, the Kasigau Massif, the Taita Hills, and western Kenya via Centrioncus aberrans (Source: Feijen & Feijen, ZooKeys 1144, 2023). No Kenya-specific occurrence or abundance dataset for stalk-eyed Diopsis is available — Kenyan presence is confirmed at the "sub-Saharan range includes Kenya" level only.

technical_sections.heading: 6. Economic / Ecological Importance
technical_sections.body: Diopsis longicornis, D. apicalis, and D. collaris are significant rice pests across sub-Saharan Africa, causing stunted growth and reduced yield, with documented yield losses in the 10–15% range (Source: Pegalepo et al., Insects 16(11):1175, 2025). D. apicalis is a common stem-boring pest causing severe yield losses in West African rice ecosystems, with damage particularly associated with wet, shady, and irrigated lowland rice (Source: Bocco et al., Insects 16(8):752, 2025). D. longicornis is characterised as the most important diopsid species affecting agriculture in the sub-Saharan African region (Source: CABI Compendium, Diopsis longicornis datasheet). Most Diopsidae, however, are saprophagous decomposers of decaying organic matter in moist habitats, a role distinct from the small number of phytophagous pest species (Source: Insect of the Week, icipe, 2023). No formal conservation-status assessment (IUCN or otherwise) was found for any Diopsidae species in whitelisted sources.

technical_sections.heading: 7. Control and Management
technical_sections.body: Cultural control includes management of alternative host plants such as goosegrass and Johnson grass, which otherwise sustain pest populations between rice-growing seasons (Source: Pegalepo et al., Insects 16(11):1175, 2025). Host-plant resistance is used as a management tool: rice variety CG14 strongly attracts D. apicalis egg-laying females but is toxic to developing larvae (antibiosis), allowing its use as a perimeter trap crop, while variety RAM55 chemically deters oviposition and can be intercropped with susceptible varieties (Source: Bocco et al., Insects 16(8):752, 2025). Chemical control options include lambda-cyhalothrin, beta-cyfluthrin, chlorantraniliprole, and imidacloprid, applied as foliar sprays at 0.25–0.5 L/ha (Source: Pegalepo et al., Insects 16(11):1175, 2025). Biological control options include the egg parasitoid Trichogramma chilonis and a Cotesia sp. larval parasitoid (Source: Pegalepo et al., Insects 16(11):1175, 2025). An integrated approach combining cultural, biological, resistant-variety, and selective chemical measures is recommended, since reliance on chemical insecticides alone provides no reliable long-term solution and affects non-target organisms (Source: Pegalepo et al., Insects 16(11):1175, 2025).

technical_sections.heading: 8. Collection Methods
technical_sections.body: No Diopsidae-specific collection methodology was found in any whitelisted source.

technical_sections.heading: 9. Notable Facts
technical_sections.body: Diopsidae is one of very few fly families in which females, not only males, bear eyestalks — in Diopsinae both sexes have eyestalks, though male eyestalks are generally longer (Source: Insect of the Week, icipe, 2023). In some Diopsidae species, eyestalk span exceeds the length of the fly's own body (Source: Insect of the Week, icipe, 2023). Approximately 65 African Diopsis species with prominent apical wing spots remain scientifically undescribed, indicating substantial unresolved taxonomic diversity within the genus in Africa (Source: Feijen & Feijen, African Invertebrates 53(1), 2012). Subfamily Centrioncinae represents a taxonomically distinct, stalkless lineage within Diopsidae restricted to African montane forest habitats, including several Kenyan mountain/forest localities — illustrating that not all Diopsidae have the stalk-eyed condition (Source: Feijen & Feijen, ZooKeys 1144, 2023).

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Meet the conehead katydid — a wedge-headed grasshopper relative that's one of the most important edible insects in East Africa. In Kenya it's part of the "senene" harvest, a katydid so valued as food that entire seasonal trades are built around catching it. Its scientific name, Ruspolia differens, ties it to a whole family of "conehead" katydids found around the world — but confusingly, the American coneheads you might read about online belong to completely different, unrelated genera. The one in this photo is the Old World, African branch of the conehead family tree.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: The name "conehead" comes from the sharply pointed, wedge-shaped head visible even in a nymph like this one — you can see it clearly in the photo, along with the huge eyes and the long, whip-thin antennae held apart in a wide V. Adults grow to about 5–6 cm long, with wings that stretch past the back legs. They come in a surprising range of colours — green, brown, and striped or blushed versions of both — and males and females look a little different from each other: males are smaller and carry a pair of odd little flap-like structures on the underside of their bodies, while females carry a long, needle-like egg-laying tube called an ovipositor.

sections.heading: How Do They Live?
sections.body: From egg to adult takes about five months. Eggs get tucked into damp grass sheaths or maize shoots, and hatch in two to three weeks depending on how wet things are. The nymphs then moult their way through several stages — six for males, seven for females — before becoming adults, feeding mostly on grass flower heads rather than leaves or stems. Twice a year, something remarkable happens: the population swarms, taking to the air in huge, astonishingly predictable mass flights, usually around April–May and again around November–December. Orthopterists consider this level of predictable, synchronized swarming unusual among grasshoppers and katydids generally.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: This is where the conehead katydid really stands out — it's food. Across more than twenty African countries, people harvest it as a protein-rich delicacy, and in parts of Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania around Lake Victoria, it's a genuine cash crop, fetching prices comparable to beef or chicken. Nutritionally, it holds up well too: it can be well over half protein by weight, rich in healthy fats, and packed with minerals. But there's a catch — some market samples have also tested positive for concerning bacteria and heavy metals, so how it's harvested, stored, and cooked really matters for safety. Deep-frying, the traditional preparation method, does a good job of cutting down the bacterial load.

sections.heading: How Are They Caught?
sections.body: Because they're strongly drawn to light at night, harvesters set up bright lamps — traditionally mercury-vapour bulbs — over oil-coated drums during the swarming seasons. The insects fly in, get disoriented, and drop straight into the collection container. A single good night at one of these traps can bring in the equivalent of eight to ten 100-kilogram sacks — a serious harvest from a creature barely a couple of inches long.

sections.heading: One Persistent Problem
sections.body: Given how valuable this insect is, you'd think farming it in captivity would have been solved long ago — but adult conehead katydids have a habit of eating each other when crowded together, and this cannibalism remains one of the biggest unsolved obstacles to scaling up commercial rearing. Researchers have found that giving them live prey, like fly larvae, cuts down on the cannibalism significantly — but for now, most of the harvest still comes from the wild swarms rather than a farm.

technical_sections.heading: 1. Taxonomy and Classification
technical_sections.body: Ruspolia differens (Serville, 1838) belongs to Order Orthoptera, Suborder Ensifera, Family Tettigoniidae, Subfamily Conocephalinae, Tribe Copiphorini, Genus Ruspolia Schulthess, 1898 (Source: Orthoptera Species File, otus/844016; GBIF Species API, api.gbif.org/v1/species/5096598). Taxonomic history: originally described as Conocephalus differens Serville, 1838, later moved through Conocephaloides differens (Kirby, 1906) and Homorocoryphus differens (Karny, 1912) before reaching its current combination, Ruspolia differens (Bailey, 1975). Other synonyms include Conocephalus vicinus Walker, 1869 and Conocephalus exiguus Stål, 1876 (Source: Orthoptera Species File). The type locality is Mauritius, with the lectotype held at the Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle, Paris (Source: Orthoptera Species File). The genus Ruspolia contains 37 accepted species (GBIF backbone taxonomy) distributed across most of the Old World, and is absent from the Americas and Antarctica (Source: GBIF Species API; Orthoptera Species File genus records). Disambiguation of the common name "conehead katydid": the same descriptive name is used independently on both sides of the Old World/New World divide. In the Americas, "conehead" refers to unrelated genera Copiphora (Mexico, Central and South America) and Neoconocephalus (Nearctic/Neotropical) — neither occurs in Kenya. Within genus Ruspolia itself, the Palearctic species R. nitidula is also called the "Large Conehead," but it is solitary, restricted to Europe/Asia/North Africa, and not the East African species. The Kenyan/East African "conehead katydid" is Ruspolia differens, distinguished from R. nitidula by its swarming behaviour and colour polymorphism (Source: Orthoptera Species File).

technical_sections.heading: 2. Morphology
technical_sections.body: Adults measure 52–60 mm in total length, with long wings extending beyond the hind knees and the tip of the ovipositor. The head bears the diagnostic conical/wedge-shaped fastigium that gives the tribe its common name (Source: Orthoptera Species File; synthesis of associated literature). Males possess a pair of tongue-like metathoracic flaps and dorsoventrally bi-lobed cerci, are smaller than females, and show male-biased antennal length. Females are identified by a long, slender ovipositor (Source: Malinga, Opoke & Rutaro, IntechOpen chapter, citing Matojo & Yarro 2010/2013). Colour polymorphism includes six recorded morphs — green, purple-striped green, purple-suffused green, brown, purple-striped brown, and purple-suffused brown — with green and brown predominating; tegmen colour is sex-linked, brown associated with males and green with females (Source: Malinga, Opoke & Rutaro, IntechOpen chapter, citing Matojo & Yarro 2010).

technical_sections.heading: 3. Biology and Life Cycle
technical_sections.body: The life cycle proceeds from egg through nymph to adult, spanning roughly 147 days in total. Nymphs pass through 6 instars in males and 7 in females; males mature faster, likely reflecting the shorter developmental path (Source: Malinga, Opoke & Rutaro, IntechOpen chapter, citing Brits & Thornton 1981). Eggs are laid in moist substrates — leaf sheaths of grasses, shoots of Panicum sp., maize seedlings, and Pennisetum sp. in the field, or cotton wool and folded plastic cloth in captivity — and hatch after 11–25 days depending on moisture (Source: Malinga, Opoke & Rutaro, IntechOpen chapter, citing Egonyu et al. 2020, Malinga et al. 2019, Hartley 1967). In mass-rearing trials, females laid roughly 2.5 times more eggs on folded plastic cloth (169.3±18.0 eggs) than on natural Pennisetum purpureum leaf sheath (69.0±13.9 eggs), though hatchability did not differ significantly between the two substrates (overall mean 56.5±4.7%) (Source: Malinga et al. 2019, Journal of Economic Entomology 112(5):2157–2160). Rearing studies establish an optimal temperature near 29°C; at 30°C, development from newly hatched nymph to adult took about 49 days with 86.7% survival, the highest recorded, while maximum adult weight (0.62 g) occurred at 28°C. Harvesting 10 days after the adult moult yielded up to 50% more biomass than immediate harvest (Source: Lehtovaara, Roininen & Valtonen 2018, Journal of Economic Entomology 111(6):2652). On host-plant-based artificial diets, development time ranged 88.8–105.9 days, adult longevity 31–42 days, adult weight 0.46–0.51 g, and fecundity reached up to 45.6 eggs per female on a Megathyrsus maximus-amended diet versus 15.8 on the control diet (Source: Leonard et al. 2022, Journal of Insect Science 22(2):8). R. differens shows a distinct swarming phase, with predictable mass flights typically occurring twice yearly in East Africa — around April–May and again around November–December — alongside a non-swarming "local population" phase whose developmental stages persist in the field year-round (Source: Malinga, Opoke & Rutaro, IntechOpen chapter, citing Matojo & Njau 2010). Cannibalism among adults is a documented behavioural trait that complicates captive mass-rearing (see Ecology, below).

technical_sections.heading: 4. Ecology
technical_sections.body: R. differens is a facultatively oligophagous grass feeder. Field surveys recorded it on 19 grass species and 2 sedge species, with 99% of nearly 21,000 feeding observations concentrated on seven grasses: Panicum maximum, Brachiaria ruziziensis, Chloris gayana, Hyparrhenia rufa, Cynodon dactylon, Sporobolus pyramidalis, and Pennisetum purpureum; Panicum maximum was the preferred host of the youngest nymphs (Source: cited in Malinga, Opoke & Rutaro, IntechOpen chapter). Feeding is highly selective for inflorescences (97% of observations) over leaves, stems, and inflorescence stalks. Cannibalism among adults reared in captivity has made mass-rearing a persistent challenge; supplying live insect prey such as black soldier fly larvae or armyworms significantly reduced cannibalistic behaviour in both sexes compared with artificial-diet controls (Source: Fombong, Tanga, Nganga, Kinyuru & Vanden Broeck 2023, Journal of Insects as Food and Feed 9(10):1309–1319, via icipe institutional repository). The species is predominantly nocturnal and strongly attracted to artificial light at night, a behaviour directly exploited in commercial harvesting (see Collection Methods, below).

technical_sections.heading: 5. Distribution and Diversity
technical_sections.body: The genus Ruspolia comprises 37 accepted species occurring across most of the Old World, absent from the Americas and Antarctica (Source: GBIF Species API; Orthoptera Species File). Ruspolia differens itself has a broad Sub-Saharan African range, with documented occurrence in Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Angola, South Africa, Ghana, Central African Republic, DR Congo, Zambia, Rwanda, Burundi, Mauritius (the type locality), Madagascar, and Ivory Coast (Source: Malinga, Opoke & Rutaro, IntechOpen chapter). Kenya and the Lake Victoria basin: the species is documented as a food resource consumed by the Luo of Kenya around the Lake Victoria basin, alongside the Baganda of Uganda and the Haya of Tanzania (Source: Malinga, Opoke & Rutaro, IntechOpen chapter). GBIF's own georeferenced occurrence records for Kenya are notably sparse, limited to a small cluster of 1990s museum specimens around Nairobi, with no georeferenced records found for western Kenya, the Lake Victoria basin, Uganda, or Tanzania — a gap in the occurrence database itself rather than evidence of absence, given the robust ecological and food-science literature documenting the species throughout this region (Source: GBIF Occurrence API queries). Scientific collecting via light trap has also documented the species in Central African Republic (Bangui, Dzanga-Sangha, Dzanga-Ndoki National Park, 2008–2012) (Source: Massa et al. 2020, Zootaxa, via Zenodo).

technical_sections.heading: 6. Economic / Ecological Importance
technical_sections.body: Ruspolia differens is one of the most economically and culturally important edible insects in East and Central Africa, consumed in over 20 African countries (Source: Malinga, Opoke & Rutaro, IntechOpen chapter; Kababu et al., Journal of Economic Entomology review). Reported protein content ranges from roughly 34–73% of dry matter, with fat 33–48%, carbohydrate 3–6%, and polyunsaturated fatty acids making up about 89% of the lipid fraction; chitin content is 10–15% (Source: Malinga, Opoke & Rutaro, IntechOpen chapter). A review found flavonoids (quercetin, luteolin) and antioxidant activity (87.00±2.59%) comparable to fruits and vegetables, but also documented food-safety concerns, including pathogenic bacteria (Clostridium, Bacillus, Staphylococcus) in market samples and heavy-metal contamination — lead and cadmium reported at roughly ten-fold above recommended thresholds in some samples — mitigated by proper processing (Source: Kababu et al., Journal of Economic Entomology review). Trade in R. differens is a primary income source for many households in the Lake Victoria basin, with market prices comparable to beef or chicken. Swarming individuals are occasionally noted as minor pests on the developing seeds of cereal crops at the milk stage, but no whitelisted source was found documenting crop-loss data or an economic damage assessment for this.

technical_sections.heading: 7. Control and Management
technical_sections.body: No whitelisted source was found treating Ruspolia differens as a pest requiring active biological, chemical, or cultural control. The species is overwhelmingly documented in the literature as an edible/farmed resource rather than a pest, and this topic area is reported here as a genuine gap in the available coverage rather than padded with unsupported material.

technical_sections.heading: 8. Collection Methods
technical_sections.body: The dominant commercial harvesting method exploits the species' strong attraction to artificial light during its two annual swarming seasons. Collectors set up light sources at night — traditionally mercury vapour bulbs positioned over oil-coated metal drums with open tops — so that disoriented insects fall into the containers; high-yield nights can reportedly produce eight to ten sacks of roughly 100 kg each. Scientific specimen collection also relies on light traps, as documented for material collected in the Central African Republic between 2008 and 2012 (Source: Massa et al. 2020, Zootaxa, via Zenodo).

technical_sections.heading: 9. Notable Facts
technical_sections.body: The name "conehead" is applied independently to Ruspolia on both sides of the Old World/New World divide — Orthoptera Species File itself labels the Palearctic Ruspolia nitidula the "Large Conehead," while the East African literature repeatedly calls R. differens the "swarming conehead" — reflecting a shared descriptive term for the wedge-shaped head rather than a single-species or single-continent name (Source: Orthoptera Species File). R. differens shows a biannual swarming phenology described in the literature as highly predictable and exceptional among Orthoptera generally, most of which do not show comparably reliable mass-flight timing. Despite decades of applied research interest in captive mass-rearing as a food-security crop insect, cannibalism remains a persistent, unresolved obstacle to scaling up farming (Source: Fombong et al. 2023, Journal of Insects as Food and Feed). The species is nutritionally comparable to or exceeding many conventional protein sources, yet market samples have also tested positive for concerning levels of heavy metals and pathogenic bacteria, highlighting a real food-safety tension in an otherwise strongly promoted food-security narrative (Source: Kababu et al., Journal of Economic Entomology review).

sections.heading: What Is It?
sections.body: This bold black-and-yellow insect is a young "hopper" (nymph) of the Elegant Grasshopper, Zonocerus elegans — a common East African grasshopper found across Kenya's savannahs, gardens, and farmland. Despite the name confusion with a similar-looking West African cousin (Zonocerus variegatus), records confirm that any black-and-yellow Zonocerus nymph spotted in Kenya is this species, not its western relative.

sections.heading: What Does It Look Like?
sections.body: Young nymphs like the one photographed are strikingly patterned in black with bold white or yellow spots and bands — a "don't eat me" warning outfit rather than camouflage. As they grow into adults, the colours shift toward a richer mix of yellow, olive, dull red, orange, and black, with orange-red eyes and antennae ringed in black and orange. Most adults keep short wings their whole lives — even the rare individuals with full-length wings are clumsy fliers, so this grasshopper gets around mostly by walking and hopping rather than flying.

sections.heading: How Does It Grow Up?
sections.body: Females lay batches of 20 to over 100 eggs in pods in the soil, timed around the rains. The eggs then wait — sometimes for six to nine months — before hatching. Young nymphs hatch out in large groups and stick together, clustering conspicuously at the tips of low plants. This "safety in numbers" habit, combined with their loud warning colours, helps deter predators. Adults are more likely to go it alone.

sections.heading: Why Is It Black and Yellow?
sections.body: Those colours are advertising, not decoration. This grasshopper (and its West African relative in particular) can produce a foul-smelling defensive fluid from glands on its body, and its bold pattern warns predators to expect an unpleasant surprise if they attack. Some Zonocerus grasshoppers go a step further: they deliberately seek out and eat plants containing toxic chemicals (pyrrolizidine alkaloids), storing the toxins in their own bodies as an extra layer of chemical defence — essentially building their own poison from what they eat.

sections.heading: What Does It Eat?
sections.body: This species is a food generalist, feeding on a huge range of plants — onions, amaranth, citrus, coffee, cassava, sweet potato, banana, tobacco, and many more. It thrives in open savannah country and avoids thick forest or true desert.

sections.heading: Why Does It Matter?
sections.body: Zonocerus grasshoppers can be a real headache for farmers — the West African relative has been blamed for cassava losses of up to half a crop in bad years, and this East African species is likewise known to nibble away at cassava yields. On the flip side, in parts of South Africa these grasshoppers are also eaten as a nutritious, protein-rich snack. Where control is needed, researchers have developed a natural fungal spray that specifically targets grasshoppers like this one, killing most of a treated population within two to three weeks without harming other wildlife.

technical_sections.heading: 1. Taxonomy and Classification
technical_sections.body: Kingdom Animalia; Phylum Arthropoda; Class Insecta; Order Orthoptera; Suborder Caelifera; Family Pyrgomorphidae; Genus Zonocerus; Species Zonocerus elegans (Thunberg, 1815) (Source: Orthoptera Species File, orthoptera.speciesfile.org). Two subspecies are recognised: Z. e. elegans and Z. e. angolensis Kevan, 1972, with listed synonyms including atriceps, brevipennis, hova, and roseipennis (Source: Orthoptera Species File). Classification is cross-confirmed by GBIF, which lists the same ranks down to species, with authority "(Thunberg, 1815)" and status ACCEPTED (Source: GBIF, gbif.org/species/7197443). The related, more westerly congener is Zonocerus variegatus (Linnaeus, 1758) (Source: GBIF, gbif.org/species/1727818; CABI Compendium 10.1079/cabicompendium.57607).

technical_sections.heading: 2. Morphology
technical_sections.body: Nymphs ("hoppers") of Z. elegans are mainly black with white or yellow markings, and the pied nymphs are gregarious (Source: CABI Compendium datasheet, "Elegant grasshopper, Zonocerus elegans", via researchgate.net author-hosted copy). Adults show aposematic colouring described as predominantly yellow, variegated in olive or bluish-green, dull red, orange and black, with red wing bases, an abdomen ringed yellow-and-black or bluish-black, orange-red eyes, a black head, and antennae alternately banded black and orange (Source: CABI Compendium). Adult females measure roughly 3.8–5.1 cm and males 3.2–4.5 cm. The species is generally brachypterous (short-winged); fully winged (macropterous) adults are comparatively rare, and even those are poor fliers (Source: CABI Compendium).

technical_sections.heading: 3. Biology and Life Cycle
technical_sections.body: Life cycle is synchronised with rainfall. Females oviposit 23–116 eggs per pod, with adults migrating to oviposition sites and depositing dense clusters of egg pods. Eggs undergo a diapause of roughly 6–9 months, depending on environmental conditions, before hatching (Source: CABI Compendium). Young nymphs are strongly gregarious, aggregating conspicuously at the tips of low vegetation; adults are less gregarious than nymphs (Source: CABI Compendium).

technical_sections.heading: 4. Ecology
technical_sections.body: Z. elegans is a savannah species that avoids dense forest and true desert. It is markedly polyphagous, with recorded host/food plants including onion, amaranth, cashew, pineapple, cruciferous crops, various Citrus, coffee, taro, cucurbits, carrot, yam, sweet potato, cassava, banana, tobacco, frangipani, and the weed Chromolaena odorata (Siam weed) (Source: CABI Compendium). Nymphs and adults produce an odorous defensive secretion from paired abdominal glands, combining with the black-and-yellow warning colouration as a joint chemical–visual antipredator strategy (Source: CABI Compendium). The genus is also documented (primarily in the sister species Z. variegatus) for pharmacophagy — actively seeking and ingesting pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs) from plants such as Chromolaena odorata for chemical defense (Source: Bernays, Edgar & Rothschild, Journal of Zoology, 1977, Wiley — bibliographic citation, full text not directly accessible).

technical_sections.heading: 5. Distribution and Diversity
technical_sections.body: Z. elegans occurs across central, eastern, and southern Africa, including Madagascar, mainly south of the equator, with its range extending into East Africa, where it is the taxon actually present (Source: CABI Compendium; Orthoptera Species File). GBIF occurrence data confirm 13 Kenyan records spanning Kajiado County (Amboseli Junction, Loitokitok, Ngong), Nakuru/Naivasha, Kiambu (Kikuyu), Makueni (Kilome), Taita Taveta (Tsavo/Voi), and Narok (Maasai Mara) between 2013 and 2026 (Source: GBIF occurrence API, api.gbif.org). By contrast, only 2 Kenyan GBIF records exist for Z. variegatus, both from a single locality (Nyakach, Kisumu County) and a single observer — consistent with the CABI note that East African Z. variegatus reports "undoubtedly correspond to confusion with Z. elegans" (Source: CABI Compendium 10.1079/cabicompendium.57607). Z. variegatus itself is native to and a major pest across West and Central Africa (Nigeria, Ghana, Togo, Ivory Coast, Cameroon, Congo-Brazzaville, Benin, Sahel) (Source: CABI Compendium 10.1079/cabicompendium.57607).

technical_sections.heading: 6. Economic / Ecological Importance
technical_sections.body: Z. elegans is documented as contributing to cassava root yield losses across parts of its African range (Source: pest-status literature, title located via search — full text not accessible). The sister species Z. variegatus is far better documented as an economically damaging pest, reported to cause up to 50% annual cassava yield loss in Nigeria, damages groundnut and vegetable crops, and has been implicated in transmitting cowpea and okra mosaic viruses and bacterial blight of cassava in West Africa (Source: CABI Compendium 10.1079/cabicompendium.57607). Both species are also consumed as food insects in parts of Africa: Zonocerus spp. (including elegans) are reported eaten in South Africa (notably Limpopo, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, North West, and Gauteng), and Z. variegatus is widely consumed in West Africa with high recorded protein content (~54.9% of edible portion) (Source: "Documenting the biodiversity of edible grasshoppers in South Africa," Biodiversity and Conservation, Springer, 2023 — bibliographic citation, full text access blocked by login wall).

technical_sections.heading: 7. Control and Management
technical_sections.body: For the Zonocerus pest complex generally, biological control using the entomopathogenic fungus Metarhizium anisopliae (commercial formulation "Green Muscle") has been developed and registered in Southern Africa — registered against brown locust in South Africa from 1998, and against desert locust/grasshoppers in nine Sahelian countries from 2001 — reported to cause 70–90% mortality in treated hopper populations within 14–20 days with limited non-target impact (Source: CABI Compendium). Management guidance for Zonocerus egg pods and early aggregated instars (targeting nymphs while still clustered near oviposition sites) is also referenced in CABI/Plantwise pest-management materials (Source: CABI Compendium / Plantwise materials, found via search index; full pages inaccessible).

technical_sections.heading: 9. Notable Facts
technical_sections.body: •  The gregarious, brightly aposematic nymphs cluster conspicuously on vegetation, combining visual warning colour with a defensive secretion from paired abdominal glands as an integrated antipredator strategy (Source: CABI Compendium). •  The genus is notable in the chemical-ecology literature for actively-sought pyrrolizidine alkaloid pharmacophagy from toxic host plants — documented in the sister species Z. variegatus feeding on Chromolaena odorata — sequestering the alkaloids for its own chemical defense, a comparatively rare strategy among Orthoptera (Source: Bernays, Edgar & Rothschild, 1977, Journal of Zoology, Wiley). •  Even fully winged ("macropterous") adults of Z. elegans are described as poor fliers, meaning the species relies on walking/hopping and gregarious defense far more than flight for survival (Source: CABI Compendium).

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: If you've ever seen a big, shiny black bee drilling a perfectly round hole into a fence post, a dead branch, or the eaves of a house, you've met a carpenter bee. They belong to the genus Xylocopa, and Kenya is home to a remarkable number of them — GBIF, the global biodiversity database, has logged over 800 sightings of carpenter bees across the country, spanning at least 15 different named species.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Carpenter bees are chunky and robust — noticeably bigger than most other bees you'll come across. People often mistake them for bumblebees, but there's one easy way to tell them apart: a bumblebee's abdomen is fuzzy all over, while a carpenter bee's abdomen is smooth, shiny, and almost hairless, like it's been polished. Males and females look slightly different too — males have a pale white or yellow patch on the face, while females' faces are solid dark.

sections.heading: How Do They Build Their Homes?
sections.body: This is where the name comes from. A female carpenter bee doesn't build a nest from scratch out of wax like a honeybee — she chews her way into solid wood, using her powerful jaws to carve out a tunnel. In one well-studied relative, females dug tunnels as deep as 40 centimetres for overwintering, and built branching networks of cells for raising young — each one stocked with a ball of pollen and nectar before being sealed shut with chewed wood pulp, like a tiny larder for the next generation. Interestingly, carpenter bees aren't quite "loners" the way people often assume. It's common for a nest to be shared by a mother and one of her daughters — one bee stays inside doing guard duty, keeping intruders out and the nest clean, while the other flies out to gather food and lay eggs. Sometimes, remarkably, the daughter can even take over the egg-laying role from her own mother.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: Carpenter bees have a superpower most bees don't: they can "buzz" pollen loose. Some flowers — tomatoes are a great example — keep their pollen locked inside tiny pores instead of leaving it out in the open. A honeybee simply can't get at it. A carpenter bee, though, grips the flower and vibrates its flight muscles so hard the pollen shakes free, like a tiny tuning fork. In studies done in Kakamega, western Kenya, this "buzz pollination" from carpenter bees produced noticeably better tomato fruit than honeybees managed — the honeybees, in fact, were caught tearing at the flowers and damaging them just to steal pollen they couldn't otherwise reach. Carpenter bees also turn out to matter a lot to French bean farming near Mount Kenya, one of the country's major smallholder export crops — a study there found that farms closer to the forest, with more carpenter bees around, produced noticeably better bean yields than farms farther away with fewer bees.

sections.heading: Any Surprising Facts?
sections.body: Not every carpenter bee plays fair. Some species have worked out a shortcut: instead of pushing into a flower the "front door" way and picking up pollen along the way, they slice a little slit straight into the base of the flower with their jaws and drink the nectar directly — no pollination service rendered. And once a carpenter bee has cut that opening, other bees, including honeybees, sometimes sneak in through the same hole afterward. One more thing worth knowing: the same tunnel a carpenter bee digs into a piece of wood doesn't get used just once. Bees can return to it and extend it year after year, generation after generation — some documented tunnels have stretched to nearly 60 centimetres long after years of reuse.
